 Background Blur (Bokeh) Calculator

 Background blur is the size of the out-of-focus disk that distant points of light become in a photograph — the quality most people mean when they say "bokeh". This calculator computes the exact blur disk for your camera and lens, in millimetres on the sensor and as a percentage of frame height.

 How to use this bokeh calculator

 Pick your camera (48 bodies in the database — the sensor dimensions are exact, not "full frame approximations"), set the lens, aperture and distances, and read the blur disk. Three things drive background blur: aperture (wider = more blur), focal length (longer = more blur), and how far behind the subject the background sits . Doubling the background distance roughly doubles the blur until it approaches the infinity value — which is why a compressed background (long lens, subject far from both you and the backdrop) blurs hardest.

 Worked example

 85 mm f/1.8, focused at 3 m, background 30 m away on full frame: blur disk = 85²·(30−3)/(1.8·3·(30−0.085)) ≈ 1.21 mm — about 5.0% of frame height . That's the classic "creamy separation" portrait look. The same lens on Micro 4/3 (17.3×13 mm sensor) gives the same 1.21 mm disk but 9.3% of frame height — the smaller sensor makes the blur look stronger relative to the frame, which is why M4/3 portraits with fast lenses still blur nicely.

 🎒 Want this as a laminated field card? The ShutterMath Field Kit has all six, print-ready.

 Background blur FAQ

 How is background blur calculated? b = f²·(x−s) / (N·s·(x−f)) with all lengths in millimetres; at infinity it simplifies to f²/(N·s). This is the standard geometric formula for the out-of-focus disk diameter on the sensor.

 What does the blur disk size mean for bokeh? As a percentage of frame height: under ~2% looks nearly sharp, 3–5% is gentle separation, 6%+ is the strong blur portrait shooters chase. The disk's edges (smooth vs. busy) are the lens's optical character — that's the part of bokeh no number can capture.

 Does sensor size affect background blur? Yes — same lens and distances, the blur disk is the same physical size, but it occupies a bigger slice of a smaller sensor's frame. That's why Micro 4/3 can look more blurred at the same settings, and why full frame "isolates" subjects with normal lenses.

 What's the difference between blur and depth of field? DoF is about what's acceptably sharp ; blur is about how soft the out-of-focus areas are. You can have a thin DoF with modest background blur (wide-angle close-up) or a deep DoF with strong blur (telephoto at f/5.6). They follow different math.

 Crop Factor Calculator

 Crop factor is the diagonal of a full frame sensor (43.27 mm) divided by the diagonal of yours. It tells you what focal length and aperture give the same picture on full frame. Enter your sensor and lens below.

 How the crop factor is calculated

 Short answer: crop factor = 43.27 mm ÷ your sensor diagonal. A Canon APS-C body is 1.61×, a Nikon or Sony APS-C body 1.53×, Micro Four Thirds 2.0× and Fujifilm GFX 0.79×. Multiply the focal length by the crop factor to get the full frame equivalent, and do the same to the f-number to compare depth of field.

 The diagonal of a 36 × 24 mm frame is √(36² + 24²) = 43.27 mm. Dividing that by your sensor's diagonal gives a single number that converts every lens you own into full frame terms:

 Focal length: 50 mm on a 1.5× body frames like 75 mm on full frame. The lens does not change; the sensor simply records a narrower part of the image circle.

 Aperture: multiply as well. An f/2 lens on Micro Four Thirds matches the depth of field of f/4 on full frame, and gathers the same total light as f/4 spread over a quarter of the area. Exposure per unit area is unchanged, which is why your meter still reads f/2.

 ISO: do not multiply. ISO is a per-area sensitivity; the smaller sensor simply has less area, which is why its low light performance is worse by roughly the same factor.

 Crop factor by sensor size

 Reference sensor dimensions and the focal length that matches a 50 mm lens on full frame

 Common questions

 Does crop factor change depth of field?

 Yes, if you frame the subject the same way. To match the framing you either move back or use a shorter lens, and both increase depth of field. The full frame camera at f/2.8 therefore separates the subject more than a 2× sensor at f/2.8. Multiply the f-number by the crop factor to compare the two fairly: f/2.8 on Micro Four Thirds equals f/5.6 on full frame.

 Is crop factor the same as zoom?

 No. Crop factor describes how much of the image circle the sensor records. A 1.5× sensor records a smaller area, so the picture looks like a longer lens was used, but the lens magnification and the perspective are unchanged. Nothing is optically zoomed.

 Does crop factor change exposure?

 No. f/2 at 1/100 s and ISO 100 gives the same brightness on any sensor size. Only the total light collected and the depth of field change, because the sensor area changes.

 How to use this depth of field calculator

 Pick your camera — the sensor size and circle of confusion are applied automatically (no more guessing your CoC).

 Select your lens or type the focal length and choose the aperture you plan to shoot at.

 Enter your focus distance (m or ft) and read the near limit, far limit, and total depth of field.

 Save setups you use often — they're stored in your browser and reload instantly next time.

 For landscape work, check the hyperfocal distance : focus there and everything from half that distance to infinity is sharp. For portraits, you'll usually want a wide aperture so the far limit stays comfortably behind your subject's head.

 Depth of field FAQ

 What is depth of field, in plain English? Depth of field is the distance range in your scene that looks acceptably sharp. Only one plane is truly in focus; everything else falls within the depth of field if it's close enough to that plane that the blur stays below the circle of confusion.

 Does sensor size change depth of field? Yes — at the same focal length and aperture, a larger sensor produces shallower depth of field because it needs a longer lens to achieve the same framing. The circle of confusion also scales with sensor diagonal, which the calculator handles automatically.

 What aperture gives maximum depth of field? Diffraction starts softening images around f/8–f/11 on full frame, f/5.6–f/8 on APS-C and Micro 4/3. The sharpest "landscape" choice is usually the smallest aperture before diffraction — use the hyperfocal distance at that aperture.

 Depth of field tables (full frame, sharpness circle 0.029 mm)

 Short answer: at 3 m with a 50 mm lens, f/8 gives a
depth of field of 1.77 m (sharp from 2.36 m to 4.12 m).
Opening up to f/1.4 shrinks that to 0.29 m; stopping down to f/16 grows it to 4.61 m.
Every figure below is computed with the same formula the calculator uses.

 Why the numbers move the way they do

 Depth of field grows with the square of focus distance, so doubling the focus distance
roughly quadruples the sharp zone at the same aperture. It shrinks with the square of focal
length, which is why an 85 mm portrait lens at f/8 has less depth than a 24 mm wide angle at
the same f/8. Aperture acts linearly: one stop down adds about 41% more depth, not double.

 The formulas behind the table are standard thin-lens equations. Hyperfocal distance is
 H = f² / (N × c) + f , where f is focal length in mm, N the f-number and
 c the circle of confusion. The near limit is H × s / (H + (s − f)) and the far
limit is H × s / (H − (s − f)) , with s the focus distance. Once s reaches
 H the far limit becomes infinity, which is the hyperfocal trick: focus at H and
everything from H/2 to infinity is acceptably sharp.

 Circle of confusion here is the sensor diagonal divided by 1500, the
classic 35 mm standard (0.029 mm on full frame). A print viewed closer than the standard
0.25 m viewing distance needs a smaller circle: divide the CoC by the same factor you enlarge
the print.

 Equivalent exposure pairs (same EV, full frame reference)

 Aperture Shutter (at ISO 100) EV100 

 f/1.4 1/1000 s 10 

 f/2.0 1/500 s 10 

 f/2.8 1/250 s 10 

 f/4.0 1/125 s 10 

 f/5.6 1/60 s 10 

 f/8.0 1/30 s 10 

 f/11 1/15 s 10 

 f/16 1/8 s 10 

 Each row captures the same amount of light (EV 10): closing the aperture one stop halves the light, so the shutter must double in length. This is the exposure triangle in its purest form. For the full explanation see the exposure triangle guide .

 Worked example

 You're shooting f/2.8 at 1/250 s, ISO 100 — the calculator reports EV ≈ 11. You want more depth of field: open to f/4 costs one stop of light, so the equivalent exposure becomes 1/125 s (one stop slower). Same EV 11, same brightness, twice the depth of field. That's the entire point of the tool: instead of guessing, set the aperture you want , read the shutter you need , and only reach for ISO when neither aperture nor shutter can move. In practice this kills the most common exposure error — changing one setting and forgetting to compensate the other.

 Exposure value FAQ

 What is exposure value (EV)? EV = log₂(N²/t) — a single number describing how much light reaches the sensor for a given aperture N and shutter time t. EV100 is the EV at ISO 100. Higher EV = brighter scene or more light collected.

 Do equivalent exposures look identical? Brightness: yes. But each parameter changes the image: aperture changes depth of field, shutter changes motion blur, ISO changes noise. Equivalence lets you trade one for another while keeping brightness constant.

 How does ISO fit into EV? ISO doesn't change the light — it changes amplification. The scene-brightness value is EV100 − log₂(ISO/100): at ISO 400 (2 stops), the same scene reads as 2 EVs lower, which is why you can shoot at 1/4 the shutter speed or 2 stops narrower aperture.

 Exposure value chart: what EV means in practice
 Short answer: EV measures the light, not the camera settings. EV 15 is bright sun, EV 8 is a lit street at night, and each EV step is one stop of shutter, aperture or ISO. At ISO 100, EV = log2(N squared / t).

 Starting exposures at ISO 100, rounded to real shutter speeds. Meter, then adjust for the subject. Scene EV at ISO 100 Start at f/2.8 Start at f/8 
 Bright sun, clear sky 16 f/2.8 at 1/8000 f/8 at 1/1000 
 Sunny, hazy or thin cloud 15 f/2.8 at 1/4000 f/8 at 1/500 
 Cloudy bright, open shade 14 f/2.8 at 1/2000 f/8 at 1/250 
 Overcast 13 f/2.8 at 1/1000 f/8 at 1/125 
 Heavy overcast, deep shade 12 f/2.8 at 1/500 f/8 at 1/60 
 Sunset, sun on the horizon 12 f/2.8 at 1/500 f/8 at 1/60 
 After sunset, warm afterglow 9 f/2.8 at 1/60 f/8 at 1/8 
 Night street with lit signs 8 f/2.8 at 1/30 f/8 at 1/4 
 Full moon 15 f/2.8 at 1/4000 f/8 at 1/500 
 Milky Way, dark sky 2 f/2.8 at 2 s f/8 at 15 s 

 Read this as a sanity check. A grey card in bright sun sits at EV 15; snow and white sand need +1 to +2 EV of compensation because the meter wants to render them grey, and a dark forest or a backlit subject needs -1 EV.
 One EV is one stop, so equivalent exposures share an EV: f/2.8 at 1/500 s, f/8 at 1/60 s and f/11 at 1/30 s are the same brightness. The calculator above converts between them without changing the exposure.

 How field of view works

 Field of view (angle of view) is set by two things: the sensor dimensions and the focal length. A 50 mm lens on full frame sees 39.6° horizontally; the same lens on APS-C sees about 25 to 27° (1.6x and 1.5x crops) — which is why crop sensors "crop" the frame (1.5× crop ≈ 75 mm equivalent).

 The 35 mm equivalent is the focal length that would give the same framing on a full-frame body. It's how photographers compare lenses across sensor sizes: Micro 4/3 has a 2× crop, APS-C ≈ 1.5× (Canon ≈ 1.6×), phones ≈ 5-7×.

 Worked example

 You're choosing a lens for an indoor shoot and the room is 4 m across. With a full-frame body, a 24 mm lens (73.7° horizontal) frames the whole wall from about 2.8 m back, while a 35 mm (54.4°) needs ~4 m — the calculator tells you exactly which lens fits before you carry it there. The same math works in reverse for video: pick your shot size, then check whether your zoom range covers it at the working distance. This is also how you compare across sensor formats — a 23 mm lens on APS-C frames like 35 mm on full frame, and the calculator shows both angles side by side.

 Field of view reference table (focal length × sensor)

 Horizontal angle of view in degrees for each focal length and sensor format. Divide-by-two, roughly: a 24 mm lens on full frame sees about 74°, and the same lens on APS-C sees about 52° — which is why a 24 mm on a crop body frames like a 36 mm on full frame.

 📐 Rule of thumb: doubling the focal length halves the angle of view. 24 mm → 74°, 48 mm → 37°, 96 mm → 18°. Equally, moving a lens from full frame to Micro 4/3 (2.0× crop) halves it again.

 Field of view FAQ

 What's the difference between FOV and focal length? Focal length is a property of the lens; field of view is the result on a given sensor. The same lens gives different FOV on different bodies. That's why "35 mm equivalent" exists.

 How is field of view calculated? FOV = 2 × atan(sensor dimension ÷ (2 × focal length)), in degrees. Horizontal uses sensor width, vertical uses height, diagonal uses the diagonal.

 Does field of view change when I crop in post? Yes — cropping changes the effective sensor area, so the FOV narrows exactly like using a longer lens. The calculator's distance fields show you the scene dimensions your final crop will cover.

 Angle of view and frame size (full frame 36 × 24 mm)

 Short answer: a 50 mm lens on a full frame body sees
39.6° across and covers 7.20 m at 10 m. A 24 mm lens sees 73.7° and covers
15.00 m at the same distance. Diagonal angle of view is the number in most lens specs;
horizontal is the one that decides whether a group or a room fits.

 Full frame. Frame size scales linearly with distance: halve the distance, halve the width. Focal length Horizontal angle Vertical angle Frame width at 10 m Frame height at 10 m 
 14 mm 104.3° 81.2° 25.71 m 17.14 m 
 16 mm 96.7° 73.7° 22.50 m 15.00 m 
 20 mm 84.0° 61.9° 18.00 m 12.00 m 
 24 mm 73.7° 53.1° 15.00 m 10.00 m 
 28 mm 65.5° 46.4° 12.86 m 8.57 m 
 35 mm 54.4° 37.8° 10.29 m 6.86 m 
 40 mm 48.5° 33.4° 9.00 m 6.00 m 
 50 mm 39.6° 27.0° 7.20 m 4.80 m 
 70 mm 28.8° 19.5° 5.14 m 3.43 m 
 85 mm 23.9° 16.1° 4.24 m 2.82 m 
 100 mm 20.4° 13.7° 3.60 m 2.40 m 
 135 mm 15.2° 10.2° 2.67 m 1.78 m 
 200 mm 10.3° 6.9° 1.80 m 1.20 m 
 300 mm 6.9° 4.6° 1.20 m 0.80 m 
 400 mm 5.2° 3.4° 0.90 m 0.60 m 

 Reading the table

 Field of view depends on the sensor, not just the lens. The same 50 mm is a normal lens on
full frame (39.5° across), a short telephoto on APS-C (25.3°, because a
1.6× body frames 50 mm like 80 mm) and a mild telephoto on Micro Four Thirds
(20.4°). Divide by the crop factor to compare focal lengths across formats.

 Angle of view is not linear with focal length, which is why the jump from 14 mm to 24 mm
looks enormous and the jump from 200 mm to 400 mm looks modest. Doubling focal length halves
the frame width; it does not halve the angle.

 How guide numbers work

 At a given ISO (traditionally 100) and zoom head setting, a flash's guide number is the product of aperture × distance that gives a correct exposure at full power : GN = f-stop × metres.

 Same GN, bigger aperture → shorter reach: GN 32 at f/2.8 reaches 11.4 m; at f/8 it reaches 4 m.

 ISO scaling: the effective GN multiplies by √2 for each ISO stop — ISO 100 → 400 (2 stops) doubles the GN, so GN 32 @ ISO 100 behaves like GN 64 @ ISO 400.

 Power fractions: ½ power reduces GN by √2 (one stop); ¼ power by 2 (two stops).

 Flash GN FAQ

 What does "GN 60 at ISO 100" actually mean? It means the flash produces correct exposure at full power when aperture × distance = 60 (metres): e.g. f/2 at 30 m, f/4 at 15 m, f/8 at 7.5 m. Real-world reach is always shorter once ceilings, modifiers, and shutter limits are factored in.

 Do softboxes and bounce reduce effective GN? Yes, a lot. A softbox typically costs 1–2 stops (GN ÷ 1.4–2), bouncing off a ceiling costs 2–4 stops. Add those losses before trusting the calculator for off-camera work.

 Why does my camera meter differently than this? TTL metering measures the actual reflected flash and is usually more accurate for close work. The GN math is the planning tool — it tells you if the flash can reach before you set anything up.

 Guide number chart: how far the flash reaches
 Short answer: distance = guide number divided by f-number. A flash with GN 60 m at ISO 100 reaches 7.5 m at f/8 and 21.4 m at f/2.8. Double the ISO and the guide number rises by 1.4 times.

 Maximum distance in metres at ISO 100 for common guide numbers. Flash f/2.8 f/4 f/5.6 f/8 
 GN 30 m 10.7 m 7.5 m 5.4 m 3.8 m 
 GN 40 m 14.3 m 10.0 m 7.1 m 5.0 m 
 GN 50 m 17.9 m 12.5 m 8.9 m 6.2 m 
 GN 60 m 21.4 m 15.0 m 10.7 m 7.5 m 

 Guide numbers are quoted at ISO 100 and a specific zoom position, usually the widest the head covers. Zooming the head concentrates the light and raises the effective guide number; a diffuser spreads it and cuts it by roughly a stop. Bounce flash loses two to three stops because the ceiling is a poor reflector.
 At ISO 400 the guide number doubles, so the same flash reaches twice as far at the same aperture. That is why high ISO plus a small aperture is the usual way to light a large room from one speedlight.

 Focus Stacking Calculator

 Focus stacking works when each frame overlaps the next by about 30%. This calculator turns your near and far limits into a frame count and a focus step, so you stop guessing at 20 shots and hoping.

 How many shots does a focus stack need?

 Short answer: divide the distance you must cover by about 70% of the depth of field each frame already gives you, then add one. At 50 mm and f/8 on full frame, covering 0.5 m to 2 m needs 9 frames, with a focus step of about 20 cm. The same range at 100 mm needs 33 frames.

 The step is the whole trick. Each frame is sharp over a slab of depth. If the next frame starts where the last one ended, the merge has nothing to blend and small alignment errors become visible bands. Overlap the slabs by 30% and the software has room to work:

 Depth per frame comes from the depth of field formula at the middle of the range, not at the near end. Depth grows with distance, so a fixed step calculated at the near end leaves the far end under-covered.

 Frame count = ceil(range ÷ step) + 1. The extra frame covers the far limit itself, where depth runs out.

 Aperture: stopping down is not a substitute. Diffraction softens every frame in the stack, and no amount of merging removes it.

 Rail versus lens: a focusing rail moves the camera and changes perspective; turning the focus ring keeps perspective fixed. For anything within about a metre, the rail gives more even steps.

 Typical stacks, full frame

 Frames at 30% overlap, 0.030 mm circle of confusion, focus ring method 
 Subject Lens and aperture Range Frames Step 

 Watch face, macro 100 mm, f/8 0.30 to 0.35 m 22 2.5 mm 

 Flower head 100 mm, f/8 0.40 to 0.52 m 23 5.6 mm 

 Product shot 50 mm, f/8 0.5 to 2 m 9 0.20 m 

 Furniture 35 mm, f/8 1 to 4 m 3 2.2 m 

 Landscape foreground 24 mm, f/5.6 0.5 to 3 m 3 1.6 m 

 Set the calculator to your own values before trusting these: the step depends on the sensor, the aperture and the distance, and a change from f/8 to f/5.6 roughly halves the depth per frame.

 Common questions

 How many photos do I need for focus stacking?

 Between 3 and 12 for most subjects. Close macro work at 100 mm needs 20 to 40 frames, because depth per frame at half a metre is only a few millimetres. A wide landscape stack needs 2 or 3.

 Can I focus stack handheld?

 Yes, if you shoot a burst and let the software align the frames. Use a 50% overlap, a shutter speed fast enough to freeze movement, and expect to discard frames where the camera drifted. Static subjects on a tripod always merge better.

 Does focus stacking work with a moving subject?

 No. The subject must be still for the whole sequence, or the merge shows ghost edges. Wind, water and people are the usual reasons a stack fails.

 camera 

 What is hyperfocal distance?

 The hyperfocal distance H is the focus distance at which the far limit of your depth of field just touches infinity. Focus closer and you lose the horizon; focus farther and you waste depth of field in front of you. It's calculated as:

 H = f² / (N × c) + f 

 where f is focal length (mm), N is the aperture number, and c is the circle of confusion (mm). For a 24 mm lens at f/8 on full frame (CoC 0.030 mm): H = 576 / 0.24 + 24 = 2,424 mm ≈ 2.42 m — focus at ~2.4 m and everything from ~1.2 m to infinity is sharp.

 Hyperfocal FAQ

 Is the hyperfocal distance the same as the infinity mark on my lens? No. The infinity mark is where distant subjects are sharp, but the near limit may be far away. Hyperfocal is the specific distance that maximizes sharpness from near to infinity — usually closer than you think.

 Does hyperfocal focusing work for wide-angle lenses only? It works for any focal length, but the numbers get impractical at longer focal lengths — a 200 mm lens at f/8 has a hyperfocal distance of ~170 m on full frame, so it's mainly useful for wide and standard lenses.

 Is hyperfocal focusing accurate enough for modern high-resolution sensors? With the standard CoC convention, hyperfocal is "acceptably sharp" for normal viewing. On high-megapixel sensors some photographers use a stricter CoC (e.g. diagonal ÷ 2000) or focus stack instead — the stricter CoC makes H roughly 33% farther.

 Hyperfocal distance chart (full frame)

 Short answer: focus at the hyperfocal distance and
everything from half that distance to infinity looks sharp. On full frame, 24 mm at f/8 is
hyperfocal at 2.51 m, so the frame is sharp from 1.25 m to infinity. A 50 mm
lens at f/8 needs 10.83 m. Wide lenses buy depth far faster than small apertures do.

 How to use the chart in the field

 Set the lens to the focal length and aperture in the left columns, then focus at the
distance in the cell. Most lenses show the distance scale on the barrel, and many have a
depth of field scale that lines up the near and far limits for you. On mirrorless bodies with
focus-by-wire lenses, use the calculator, then set focus with focus peaking or by
half-pressing on an object at that distance.

 Two rules of thumb are worth memorising: halving the focal length quarters the hyperfocal
distance, and opening one stop doubles it. That is why a 16 mm at f/8 is sharp from
0.56 m to infinity once focused at 1.12 m, while a 135 mm at
the same aperture needs 79 m of focus distance before infinity is in reach.

 Hyperfocal focusing trades some sharpness at the subject for sharpness at
infinity. For a landscape with a close foreground, focus slightly beyond the hyperfocal
distance (about one third into the scene) rather than exactly at it.

 Free Macro Depth of Field Calculator

 Depth of field at macro magnifications is the narrow band of sharpness around the focus point — so thin that effective aperture and stacking step size matter as much as the f-number. At macro distances the normal DoF formulas break down — magnification takes over. This calculator uses the magnification-based approximation, reports your effective aperture , and gives you the exact focus-stacking step size .

 🔬 Reading: at your total DoF is — thinner than paper. To photograph a whole insect, shoot a stack: move focus between frames (overlap 20–30% for safety), then merge in Helicon Focus or Photoshop.

 Why macro DoF is different

 At 1:1 magnification, depth of field is roughly DoF ≈ 2·N·c·(m+1)/m² — it scales with the square of magnification, which is why 2:1 has about a quarter of the DoF of 1:1 at the same f-stop. Two practical consequences:

 Stopping down barely helps. f/16 at 1:1 gives ~1.9 mm of DoF on full frame — and diffraction (plus effective-aperture light loss) is already visible.

 Effective aperture widens. At 1:1 the effective aperture is 2 stops slower than set: f/8 set = f/16 effective. Your meter and exposure need the compensation, which is why macro images look underexposed at high magnification.

 Macro DoF FAQ

 Why is my sharp area so thin even at f/16? Because DoF falls with the square of magnification. At 2:1, f/16 gives under 1 mm. Diffraction also erodes sharpness beyond ~f/11 effective — which is exactly why macro photographers focus-stack instead of stopping down.

 What does effective aperture mean for exposure? The effective aperture is N × (1 + m). At 1:1 it's two stops narrower than set, so your camera's through-the-lens metering compensates automatically — but manual flash calculations must add those stops or your macro shots come out dark.

 How do I choose a stacking step size? Move focus by roughly 80% of the DoF per frame (the calculator's step uses this with safety overlap). Too big → gaps that even software can't stitch; too small → hundreds of redundant frames.

 Moon Exposure Calculator

 Moon exposure is the shutter speed that correctly exposes the moon's surface — and it follows a fixed rule, because the moon is simply a sunlit subject at a known brightness. This calculator applies the Looney 11 rule with phase adjustments to give you the exact settings.

 How to use this moon exposure calculator

 Pick the moon's phase and your ISO, and the calculator returns the shutter speed at your chosen aperture. The math: a full moon is a sunlit surface worth about EV 13.6 — the Looney 11 baseline (f/11 at 1/ISO). Each phase step dims the lit surface by roughly one stop. Meter with spot mode directly on the moon if your camera supports it; the Looney 11 numbers are the failsafe when the meter lies (it will, because the sky around the moon is black).

 Worked example

 A full moon at ISO 100, f/11: Looney 11 gives 1/100 s . Shoot the same moon at ISO 400 and you'd use 1/400 s (or f/22 at 1/100 s). A quarter moon is two stops dimmer: at ISO 100, f/8, that's about 1/50 s . Handheld is fine for the moon — at these shutter speeds camera shake is rarely the problem; a tripod matters when you zoom to 300 mm+ or shoot the moon with a landscape.

 Moon exposure FAQ

 What is the Looney 11 rule for moon photography? Looney 11 (the moon's equivalent of sunny 16): full moon at f/11, shutter 1/ISO. At ISO 100 that's 1/100 s at f/11 — the moon is a sunlit subject, so it needs a daylight exposure, not a night exposure.

 How do I expose the moon at different phases? Start from full moon (f/11 at 1/ISO). Add one stop for gibbous, two for quarter, three to four for a crescent — the lit fraction of the face gets dimmer as it narrows.

 Why is my moon overexposed when I shoot at night? Your camera meters the dark sky and stretches the exposure — but the moon itself is sunlit and bright. Meter directly off the moon (spot mode) or use the Looney 11 settings and let the sky go black.

 Can I photograph the moon and landscape in one shot? The moon is about 12 stops brighter than a blue-hour landscape, so one exposure can't hold both. Shoot two frames and blend, or catch a crescent moon in twilight, which is much closer in brightness.

 How to use this ND filter calculator

 Pick the closest scene preset, or type the shutter time you'd get without a filter at your aperture and ISO. Set the shutter speed you want for your shot. The calculator counts the stops between them and recommends the filter — rounding up to a real filter strength, because buying a filter one stop stronger than needed is safer than one stop weaker (you can always open the aperture or lower the ISO to compensate).

 Worked example

 Bright sun at f/8, ISO 100 (sunny 16 → EV 15): your base exposure without a filter is about 1/500 s. You want a 2-second exposure to smooth a waterfall: that's log₂(500×2) ≈ 10 stops → grab an ND1000 , which gives exactly 2 s at 1/500 s base. Want 30 s instead? Add 4 more stops — an ND1000 plus a 2-stop ND4 stacked, or a single ND16000.

 ND filter FAQ

 How do I know which ND filter I need? Meter the scene without a filter (or use the scene presets), decide the shutter time you want, then count the stops between them: every 3 stops ≈ 8× the exposure time. A 6-stop filter (ND64) is the all-rounder for daylight waterfalls; 10 stops (ND1000) for midday mist.

 What does each ND filter do? ND8 (3 stops) — gentle motion blur in shade. ND64 (6 stops) — moving water at dusk or in bright light. ND1000 (10 stops) — cotton-soft water at midday, empty streets. ND100000 (17 stops) — blackout-style exposures in full sun.

 Should I buy a fixed ND or a variable ND? Fixed filters give consistent colour and sharpness — best for landscape. Variable (VND) filters are convenient for video and run-and-gun, but can show X-shaped darkening at the wide end and are less colour-accurate.

 Can I stack ND filters? Yes — stops add: ND64 + ND8 = 9 stops. Watch for vignetting on wide lenses and a slight colour cast with cheap glass; a single filter is always optically better.

 Worked example

 Say you're shooting a waterfall at 1/125 s and want silky motion blur. Stack an ND1000 (10 stops): 1/125 × 2¹⁰ = 8.2 seconds — set the calculator to ND1000 and it shows exactly that. The pattern to internalize: every 3 stops ≈ 8× the shutter time (ND8 at 1/125 → ~1 s), every 10 stops ≈ 1000×. That's why ND64 (6 stops) is the "moving water at dusk" filter and ND1000 (10 stops) is the "bright midday" filter. Shooting in aperture priority, the camera meters through the filter, so the calculator's real job is telling you before you compose whether the resulting time is 2 s (nice streaks) or 30 s (cotton-candy water).

 ND filter FAQ

 Why does shutter time double with every stop? Each ND stop halves the light reaching the sensor, so the shutter must stay open twice as long to record the same exposure: 1/60 s at 1 stop becomes 1/30 s, 1/15 s, 1/8 s… With a 10-stop ND1000, a 1/60 s base becomes 1/60 × 2¹⁰ = ~17 s.

 What ND strength should I buy first? ND64 (6 stops) or ND1000 (10 stops) are the two most useful. ND64 suits moving water at mid-day; ND1000 is the classic choice for long exposures of 15–30 s in daylight.

 Does stacking two filters add their stops? Yes — optical densities add, so ND8 (3 stops) + ND64 (6 stops) = 9 stops total. Watch for vignetting and color cast when stacking.

 ND filter chart: stops to shutter speed
 Short answer: each stop doubles the exposure time. A 10 stop filter multiplies a 1/15 s exposure by 1024, which is 68 seconds. A 3 stop filter turns 1/60 s into 1/8 s.

 Exposure multiplication for each ND strength. The name is the transmission, so ND1000 passes 1/1000 of the light. Strength Filter name Light factor 1 s becomes 1/15 s becomes 
 1 stop ND2 2x 2 s 1/8 
 2 stops ND4 4x 4 s 1/4 
 3 stops ND8 8x 8 s 0.5 s 
 4 stops ND16 16x 16 s 1 s 
 5 stops ND32 32x 32 s 2 s 
 6 stops ND64 64x 1 min 4 s 
 7 stops ND128 128x 2 min 9 s 
 8 stops ND256 256x 4 min 17 s 
 9 stops ND512 512x 9 min 34 s 
 10 stops ND1000 1024x 17 min 1 min 
 13 stops ND8000 8192x 137 min 9 min 
 15 stops ND32000 32768x 546 min 36 min 

 Filter names and stops are often confused. ND8 is 3 stops, not 8. ND1000 is 10 stops, and some makers label it ND3.0 or 10 stop. The number after ND is the transmission factor, and stops = log2(factor).
 Stacking filters adds stops: a 6 stop and a 3 stop together give 9 stops, a factor of 512. Add the stops, never the filter names. Vignetting and colour cast grow with the stack, so prefer one strong filter.

SUMMARY: Free astro pixel scale calculator: arcseconds per pixel for any camera and lens, with the 1–2″/px sweet spot for sharp stars. Popular astro cameras included.

Home › Astro Pixel Scale Calculator 
 Free Astro Pixel Scale Calculator

 Pixel scale is the angular size of one sensor pixel on the sky, measured in arcseconds per pixel — the number that decides whether your camera can resolve stars. Image scale = 206.265 × pixel size (µm) ÷ focal length (mm) . The result, in arcseconds per pixel, tells you whether your seeing, tracking, and optics are matched to your sensor.

 Your setup

 Camera 

 Focal length (mm) 

 Pixel size (µm) 

 Typical seeing (arcsec FWHM) 
 Excellent (1.5″) Good (2.0″) 
 Average (3.0″) Poor (4.0″) 

 Result

 Pixel scale
 —
 arcsec / pixel

 Seeing sampling
 —
 pixels per seeing disk

 Verdict
 —
 for sharp round stars

 🔭 The 1–2″/px rule: most amateur setups land between 1 and 2 arcseconds per pixel — a good match for typical seeing (2″) and common mounts. Below ~0.5″/px you're oversampling (huge files, no new detail, tracking demands explode); above ~4″/px you're undersampling (blocky stars, wasted resolution).

 Why pixel scale matters

 Pixel scale determines how much sky each pixel covers. It's the single best number for judging whether a camera + lens/telescope pairing makes sense before you buy:

 Undersampled (&gt; 3–4″/px): stars land on single pixels — square, blocky stars that don't improve with more exposure.

 Sweet spot (1–2″/px): several pixels across each star image; good for most mounts and skies.

 Oversampled (&lt; 0.7″/px): the optics or seeing can't deliver that detail — you collect noise and huge files for nothing, and tracking errors become visible.

 Rule of thumb: pixel scale ≈ seeing ÷ 3 gives near-critical sampling. With 2″ seeing that's ~0.67″/px — most hobbyists choose slightly coarser to keep guiding easy.

 Pixel scale FAQ

 What's the formula for pixel scale? Pixel scale (″/px) = 206.265 × pixel size (µm) ÷ focal length (mm). Example: a camera with 3.8 µm pixels behind a 400 mm lens gives 206.265 × 3.8 ÷ 400 ≈ 1.96″/px.

 Is smaller pixel scale always better? No. Below the seeing limit you're oversampling — more pixels per star than the atmosphere delivers. The result is larger files, longer exposures for the same signal, and stricter guiding for zero real resolution gain.

 How do I find my camera's pixel size? Pixel size = sensor height (mm) × 1000 ÷ vertical resolution. ShutterMath stores this for every camera in the list automatically — just pick your camera.

 How to use this print planner

 Worked example

 A 40×60 cm gallery print at 300 DPI: 40 cm ≈ 15.7 in and 60 cm ≈ 23.6 in, so you need 15.7×300 × 23.6×300 = 4724 × 7087 px — about 33.5 MP .  Print resolution FAQ

 How many megapixels do I need for printing? It depends on print size and viewing distance. A 10×8-inch print held in the hand needs about 7 MP (300 DPI); a 40×60 cm wall print viewed from a metre away needs only about 3 MP (150 DPI). More pixels than needed only add file size, not visible quality.

 What DPI should I print at? 300 DPI for small prints viewed up close, 240 for typical wall prints, 150 is plenty for large prints viewed from a metre or more. Viewing distance is the real driver — beyond about a metre the eye can't resolve 300 DPI.

 Can I print larger than my camera's megapixels allow? Yes — modern upscaling (including AI upscalers) handles +50% gracefully for large prints, and the viewing-distance rule means large prints are forgiving. The planner shows exactly how far above native resolution you'd be.

 What DPI do you actually need?

 300 DPI — the fine-art standard for prints viewed up close (A4 and smaller).

 240 DPI — the typical photo-lab ceiling; most labs print at this and it's indistinguishable from 300 in practice.

 150 DPI — perfectly fine for large wall prints and canvases viewed from arm's length or more. A 24 MP camera prints 40×27 in at 150 DPI.

 Below ~100 DPI — softness becomes visible at normal viewing distances; resize with care.

 Print resolution FAQ

 Can I print bigger than the calculator says? Yes — software upscaling (or the lab's own upscaler) can print any size; the calculator shows the size at which every pixel maps cleanly to the DPI grid. Most labs upsample to 300 DPI automatically, and modern AI upscalers make modest enlargements invisible.

 Is 300 DPI always better than 150 DPI? For the same print size, higher DPI means more detail only if the viewing distance is close. A 40-inch print viewed from 6 feet at 150 DPI looks identical to 300 DPI to most eyes. Choose DPI by viewing distance, not by the maximum number.

 What DPI should I use for a canvas or metal print? Canvas: 150 DPI is the norm (the texture hides detail anyway). Metal and acrylic: 240–300 DPI recommended since they're glossy and often viewed close.

 How many megapixels a print size needs
 Short answer: multiply inches by dots per inch. An 8 x 10 in print at 300 dpi needs 2400 x 3000 pixels, which is 7.2 megapixels. At 150 dpi the same print needs only 1.8 megapixels, and at normal viewing distance that is still sharp.

 300 dpi is the print industry default for anything held in the hand. Wall prints are viewed from further away, so 240 dpi covers a 16 x 20 and 150 dpi is acceptable at 24 x 36 when the print hangs behind a sofa. What matters is pixels per degree of view, not a fixed number.
 Upscaling adds pixels, not detail. If the calculator says you are short by a factor of two, a sharper lens, a longer exposure on a tripod or a stitched panorama will do more than any resize algorithm.

 Free Shutter Angle Calculator

 Shutter angle expresses shutter speed as a fraction of the frame interval, with 360° being one full frame. In video, shutter speed is described as an angle. The cinematic standard — the 180° rule — sets the shutter to 1/(2 × frame rate) : 1/48 s at 24 fps, 1/60 s at 30 fps, 1/120 s at 60 fps. That's the natural motion blur your eye expects.

 Worked example

 You're shooting 24 fps and want the standard cinematic look: enter 180°, and the calculator returns 1/48 s — the classic rule (shutter = 1/(2×fps)). Switch to 60 fps for slow motion and it becomes 1/120 s. Now the creative choices: 360° (1/24 s) adds motion blur for dreamy pans, while 90° (1/96 s) makes action crisper and more staccato. Videographers memorize 180° because it sits at the sweet spot — enough blur for smooth motion, enough edge for detail. The calculator removes the mental math when you're juggling frame rates, resolutions and ND filters on set.

 Shutter angle FAQ

 Why 180 degrees? Shutter angle describes how long the shutter stays open per frame, as a fraction of a full rotation. At 180° it's open half the frame time, giving motion blur that matches how the eye tracks movement — too open (360°) blurs, too closed (45°) stutters.

 What shutter speed for slow motion? Same rule: 1/(2 × fps). At 120 fps that's 1/240 s. Many cameras auto-set this when you select 180° in video mode — check your menu.

 Does the 180° rule apply to stills? No — stills use shutter speed directly (1/focal length or faster for handheld). The angle system is a video/cinema convention, though the motion-blur logic is the same.

 Shutter speed by frame rate and shutter angle

 Short answer: the 180° shutter rule sets exposure
time to half the frame interval, so 24 fps gives 1/48 s, 30 fps gives 1/60 s and 60 fps gives
1/120 s. Multiply the frame rate by 360 and divide by the shutter angle to get the exact
speed: 24 × 360 / 180 = 48.

 Exact shutter speed. Cameras display the nearest standard value, so 23.976 fps at 180° shows 1/48. Frame rate 360° 180° 90° 45° 
 23.976 fps 1/24 s 1/48 s 1/100 s 1/200 s 
 24 fps 1/24 s 1/48 s 1/100 s 1/200 s 
 25 fps 1/25 s 1/50 s 1/100 s 1/200 s 
 29.97 fps 1/30 s 1/59 s 1/125 s 1/250 s 
 30 fps 1/30 s 1/59 s 1/125 s 1/250 s 
 48 fps 1/48 s 1/100 s 1/200 s 1/333 s 
 50 fps 1/50 s 1/100 s 1/200 s 1/333 s 
 59.94 fps 1/59 s 1/125 s 1/250 s 1/500 s 
 60 fps 1/59 s 1/125 s 1/250 s 1/500 s 
 120 fps 1/125 s 1/250 s 1/500 s 1/1000 s 
 180 fps 1/167 s 1/333 s 1/1000 s 1/1000 s 
 240 fps 1/250 s 1/500 s 1/1000 s 1/1000 s 

 Why 180° is the default

 A 180° shutter gives motion blur that matches how the eye reads movement at 24 fps. Narrow
the angle (90°, 45°) and you get crisper frames that survive slow motion and look like Saving
Private Ryan; open it to 360° and motion smears, which suits dream sequences and low light.

 Frame rate and shutter angle together decide whether lights flicker. At 50 Hz mains, shoot
25 or 50 fps; at 60 Hz, shoot 30 or 60 fps. On mixed or unknown lighting, a narrow angle lets
you keep 24 fps without banding.

TITLE: Free 500 Rule & NPF Calculator | ShutterMath
SUMMARY: Free star trails calculator: max shutter time for sharp stars via the 500/400/300 rules and the accurate NPF rule, using your camera's crop factor and pixel size.

Home › Star Trails Calculator 
 Free 500 Rule & NPF Calculator

 The 500 rule is the classic formula for the maximum shutter time before stars streak: 500 divided by the full-frame-equivalent focal length. The maximum shutter time before stars visibly trail — computed three ways: the classic 500 rule, the stricter 300 rule for high-res sensors, and the NPF rule , which accounts for your camera's actual pixel size and aperture.

 Your setup

 Camera 

 Focal length (mm) 

 Aperture (f/) 

 Target declination (0° = celestial equator) Stars near the celestial pole move slower — NPF relaxes by up to 2× at ±60°. LonelySpeck-style declination-aware calculation.

 Max exposure times

 NPF rule (accurate)
 —
 pixel-size aware

 500 rule
 —
 classic, forgiving

 300 rule
 —
 safer for high-res

 600 rule
 —
 forgiving, film-era

 🌌 How to use it: set your shutter to (or just under), open the aperture fully, then raise ISO until the histogram is ⅓–½ from the left. Check at 100% zoom: if stars are still elongated, shorten by 20%.

 Worked example

 A 20 mm lens on a Sony A1 II (full frame, 4.17 µm pixels) at f/2: the 500 rule says 500/20 = 25 s , but the NPF rule — which accounts for your real pixel size — says (35×2 + 30×4.17) / 20 ≈ 9.8 s . That's the difference between tack-sharp stars at 100% zoom and faint trails you only notice in post. Use the 500 rule as a quick mental check, but trust NPF on a modern high-resolution sensor; if you're shooting 135 mm+, even NPF gets aggressive and the calculator's pixel-scale number (arcseconds per pixel) tells you whether your rig can actually resolve stars at all.

 Which rule should you use?

 NPF rule — the accurate one. Formula: t = (35·N + 30·p) / f, where N is aperture, p is pixel size in µm, and f is the full-frame equivalent focal length. It accounts for both your sensor's pixel density and lens speed. Use this.

 500 rule — t = 500 / (focal × crop). Fine for older, lower-resolution sensors; visibly trails on 24 MP+ cameras at 100% view.

 300 rule — t = 300 / (focal × crop). A safer general choice for modern high-res sensors.

 All three assume you're shooting away from the celestial poles; pointing near Polaris (or Sigma Octantis) lets you push times 2–3× longer before trails appear.

 Star exposure FAQ

 Why do stars trail at long exposures? The Earth rotates ~15°/hour. A longer shutter moves each star across more pixels; when the movement exceeds about one pixel (or the pixel-size tolerance in NPF), the star becomes a streak instead of a point.

 Does the 500 rule still work on my 45 MP camera? Poorly — it was calibrated for 12–16 MP sensors. At 45 MP the pixels are ~4.4 µm and trails are visible well before 500/f. The NPF rule (or 300/f) is the right choice for modern sensors.

 What if I want star trails on purpose? Then ignore all rules — stack many long exposures (30 s–5 min each) and composite. The calculator's job is the opposite: keeping stars as points.

 Time Lapse Calculator

 A time lapse is just arithmetic: clip length × frame rate gives the photos you need, and photos × interval gives the time you must stand there. Set any three values below and the fourth follows.

 Cinema habit: use an interval a whole multiple of the interval at which the scene changes. Quick clouds 1 to 3 s, sunsets 3 to 10 s, shadows 30 to 60 s, stars 15 to 30 s.

 Speed up

 × real time

 at this interval

 How the numbers work

 Short answer: photos = clip length × frame rate. Shooting time = photos × interval. A 10 second clip at 24 fps needs 240 photos, which at a 2 second interval takes 8 minutes of real time, a 48× speed up.

 Photos: 10 s × 24 fps = 240 frames. Round up, always, because a clip one frame short shows as a stutter at the end.

 Shooting time: 240 × 2 s = 480 s = 8 minutes. The interval is measured from the start of one exposure to the start of the next, so add your shutter speed to the interval if the camera cannot overlap them.

 Speed up: shooting time ÷ clip length. 8 minutes into 10 seconds is 48×.

 Long exposures: if the exposure is longer than the interval, the interval becomes the exposure. Keep exposures under half the interval or the camera never returns to the start position in time.

 Common clips worked out

 Photos and shooting time at 24 fps, with the interval needed to fit a fixed window 
 Clip (24 fps) Photos 2 s interval 5 s interval 10 s interval 30 s interval 

 5 seconds 120 4 min 10 min 20 min 1 h 0 min 

 10 seconds 240 8 min 20 min 40 min 2 h 0 min 

 15 seconds 360 12 min 30 min 1 h 0 min 3 h 0 min 

 20 seconds 480 16 min 40 min 1 h 20 min 4 h 0 min 

 30 seconds 720 24 min 1 h 0 min 2 h 0 min 6 h 0 min 

 Common questions

 What interval should I use for a sunset time lapse?

 3 to 10 seconds. At a 5 second interval a 10 second clip needs 240 photos and 20 minutes of shooting, which covers the gap between the sun touching the horizon and the afterglow fading. Shorter clips of 4 to 6 seconds are often enough for social media.

 How many photos do I need for a 10 second time lapse?

 240 at 24 fps, 250 at 25 fps, 300 at 30 fps and 600 at 60 fps. Shoot about 10% extra so you can trim frames where someone walked into the shot.

 Does the interval include the exposure time?

 On most cameras the interval is the start to start time. If your shutter speed is 1 s and the interval is 1 s, the camera drops frames. Keep the exposure at or below half the interval, and turn off long exposure noise reduction, which doubles the black frame time.

 🎬 Reading: at fps your 180° shutter is . In daylight you need of neutral density — grab the . Variable NDs are the videographer's favorite for exactly this reason.

 Why video needs ND filters

 Stills photographers "fix" bright scenes with shutter speed and aperture. Videographers can't:

 Shutter is locked by the 180° rule (1/48 s at 24 fps) — the motion blur is the look.

 Aperture is limited — stop past f/8–f/11 and diffraction softens the image; plus you often want f/2.8 for shallow depth of field.

 ISO bottom is limited — most cameras go to ISO 100, and going "below base" is impossible.

 With a fixed 1/48 s shutter at base ISO in sunlight, the only thing left between you and overexposure is glass in front of the lens. A 6–10 stop variable ND covers nearly every daylight situation.

 Video ND FAQ

 What ND strength should a videographer buy first? A variable ND 2–5 or 6–9 stops covers daylight at typical apertures. Pair it with a fixed ND64 (6 stops) for the rare case you need repeatable settings. Avoid cheap variables — they cause X-pattern color cast at the dark end.

 Does the calculator work for log / flat profiles? Mostly — log profiles change the exposure curve but not the light math. You may find you need ⅓–⅔ stop more ND when exposing-to-the-right for log; check the histogram and add a third-stop if the highlights clip.

 What if my base exposure is between two filters? Split the difference: open the aperture ⅓–½ stop, drop ISO one step if you're above base, or use a variable ND. The calculator shows the closest filter and the gap — a gap under ⅓ stop is usually fine.

Home › About 
 About ShutterMath

 ShutterMath exists because the tools photographers actually use are frozen in time. The depth-of-field calculator that ranks #1 in most searches has a camera database that stops around 2013 — it has never heard of mirrorless cameras, let alone the phone in your pocket. We built the version we wanted to use: accurate math, a camera list that includes what you can buy today, and results you can print and take into the field.

 What we're trying to fix

 Outdated camera data. Every calculator on this site uses the exact sensor dimensions of your camera — full frame, APS-C, Micro 4/3, and phone sensors included — with the standard circle-of-confusion convention (sensor diagonal ÷ 1500).

 Black-box math. All formulas are the standard published ones (hyperfocal H = f²/(N·c) + f, ND time = base × 2^stops, GN = aperture × distance, pixel scale = 206.265 × µm ÷ mm), and we show them on the page so you can verify every result.

 Nothing to install. These are plain web pages — they work on any device, load fast, and run entirely in your browser. Your saved setups live in your browser's local storage; we never see them.

 Who runs this

 ShutterMath is an independent, single-operator project. We're photographers first — the site is funded by unobtrusive advertising (only after your consent, and only where it doesn't get in the way of the tools) so it can stay free, fast, and independent.

 Questions, corrections, or a camera we're missing? Get in touch — we add new cameras and tools regularly.

 Our principles

 Accuracy first. If a number is wrong, that's a bug — report it and we'll fix it.

 Free forever. No accounts, no paywalls, no watermarks on printable cheat sheets.

 Privacy by default. No tracking without consent; no data leaves your browser except what's needed to serve the page.

 Useful without ads. Every tool works fully with ads blocked or declined. Ads only ever sit in clearly marked slots, never over the controls.

SOURCE: https://shuttermath.com/pages/aperture-explained.html
TITLE: Aperture Explained: f-Stops, Depth of Field &amp; Light | Shut…
SUMMARY: Aperture explained simply: what f-stops mean, why the numbers are 1.4, 2, 2.8, 4…, how aperture controls light and depth of field, and the best f-stop for every.

Home › Guides › Aperture Explained 
 Aperture Explained

 What f-stops mean, why the numbers are 1.4, 2, 2.8, 4…, how aperture controls light and depth of field — and the best f-stop for every genre.

 Aperture is the hole in your lens that lets light through. It does exactly two things: controls how much light reaches the sensor , and controls how much of the scene is sharp (depth of field). Everything else in photography is built on those two.

 What the f-number means

 The f-number is focal length ÷ aperture diameter . A 50 mm lens at f/2 has a 25 mm opening; at f/8 it's a 6.25 mm opening. Confusingly, smaller numbers = wider openings = more light. Each full stop doubles the light, and because the opening is a circle (area = πr²), the diameter must multiply by √2 ≈ 1.414 to double the area. That's why the scale looks like this:

 f-stop f/1 f/1.4 f/2 f/2.8 f/4 f/5.6 f/8 f/11 f/16 f/22 f/32 

 Light vs f/1 1× 1/2 1/4 1/8 1/16 1/32 1/64 1/128 1/256 1/512 1/1024 

 Relative DoF 1× 1.4× 2× 2.8× 4× 5.6× 8× 11× 16× 22× 32× 

 To trade one stop of aperture, you trade one stop of shutter or ISO. The free exposure calculator does these trades for you.

 What aperture does to your photos

 Wide open (f/1.2–f/2.8): lots of light, thin depth of field, dreamy backgrounds — but only a sliver of the subject is sharp, and edges may be soft.

 Middle (f/4–f/8): the sharpest range on most lenses, still decent blur, enough light for most situations.

 Stopped down (f/11–f/22): maximum depth of field, but light drops fast and diffraction starts softening detail past f/8–f/11.

 Best aperture by genre

 Genre Typical aperture Why 

 Portrait f/1.8–f/2.8 Background blur, subject separation 

 Landscape f/8–f/11 Front-to-back sharpness without diffraction 

 Real estate f/8 Room-wide sharpness, sharpest setting 

 Street / travel f/4–f/8 Balance of blur, sharpness and light 

 Sports / action f/2.8–f/4 Fast shutter needs light; keep some DoF for focus errors 

 Astro f/1.4–f/2.8 Maximum light for stars 

 Macro f/8–f/16 Thin DoF at high magnification; stop down or stack

 Aperture, shutter and ISO as one system.

 Aperture FAQ

 What does f-stop mean? The f-number is focal length ÷ aperture diameter. Lower number = wider opening = more light, shallower depth of field.

 Why are f-stops 1.4, 2, 2.8, 4? Each stop doubles the light; area doubles, so diameter multiplies by √2 ≈ 1.414. The scale: 1, 1.4, 2, 2.8, 4, 5.6, 8, 11, 16, 22, 32.

 What's the sharpest aperture? Usually f/4–f/8 on full frame — after that, diffraction softens pixels. See the diffraction guide for your camera's exact limit.

 Does a wider aperture mean better photos? Not automatically. It means more light and more blur — and less of the scene in focus, plus softer edges wide open.

SOURCE: https://shuttermath.com/pages/camera-sensor-sizes.html
TITLE: Camera Sensor Sizes Compared | ShutterMath
SUMMARY: Camera sensor sizes compared: full frame, APS-C, Micro 4/3, 1-inch and phone sensors with exact dimensions, crop factors, and what each means.

Home › Guides › Camera Sensor Sizes 
 Camera Sensor Sizes Compared

 Exact dimensions, crop factors, and what actually changes when you move between formats.

 The formats, side by side

 Format Width × height (mm) Diagonal (mm) Crop factor Area vs full frame Typical cameras 

 Full frame 36 × 24 43.3 1.0× 100% Sony A7 IV, Canon R5 II, Nikon Z8, Panasonic S5 II 

 APS-C (Sony/Nikon/Fuji) 23.5 × 15.6 28.2 1.5× ~42% Sony A6700, Fujifilm X-T5, Nikon Z50 II 

 APS-C (Canon) 22.3 × 14.9 26.8 1.6× ~39% Canon EOS R7, R10 

 Micro 4/3 17.3 × 13 21.6 2.0× ~26% Panasonic G9 II / GH7, OM System OM-1 II 

 1-inch 13.2 × 8.8 15.9 2.7× ~13% Compact cameras, some drones 

 Phone main (~1/1.28″) 9.8 × 7.3 12.2 ~3.5× ~8% iPhone 16 Pro, Galaxy S25 Ultra, Pixel 9 Pro 

 What the crop factor actually means

 The 35 mm equivalent focal length is the focal length that gives the same framing on full frame. A 24 mm lens on APS-C (1.5×) frames like 36 mm on full frame; a 25 mm on Micro 4/3 (2×) frames like 50 mm. Our field of view calculator shows this for any combination.

 Equivalent framing is not the same as equivalent look : at the same framing and aperture, the larger sensor gives shallower depth of field (see the portrait guide ) and gathers more total light.

 Real differences that matter

 Depth of field: for the same framing and f-stop, full frame has the shallowest DoF — that's the classic "full frame bokeh" advantage. Check the numbers with the DoF calculator .

 Low light: at the same exposure settings, the larger sensor collects more light overall, which typically means less noise when you normalize for print size.

 Size and reach: crop sensors give extra telephoto reach (a 400 mm lens on APS-C frames like 600 mm) in a smaller, lighter kit — one reason wildlife shooters choose APS-C and Micro 4/3.

 Hyperfocal distance: smaller sensors have shorter hyperfocal distances, making "everything sharp" landscapes easier (see the hyperfocal chart ).

 Sensor size FAQ

 Is a full-frame sensor always better? Better for low light and shallow DoF, yes — but it costs more, weighs more, and needs bigger lenses. APS-C and Micro 4/3 win on reach, size, and price. "Better" depends on what you shoot.

 What does "crop factor 1.5×" mean for my 50 mm lens? It frames like a 75 mm lens on full frame. The lens itself doesn't change — the smaller sensor just captures a narrower part of its image circle.

 Do phone cameras really have 1/1.28-inch sensors? Yes — the main cameras in current flagships use sensors around 9.8 × 7.3 mm (about 8% of a full-frame area). The "1/1.28″" naming is an old vidicon-tube convention, which is why the actual dimensions look surprising.


------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SOURCE: https://shuttermath.com/pages/circle-of-confusion.html
TITLE: Circle of Confusion Explained | ShutterMath
SUMMARY: What circle of confusion (CoC) is, why calculators disagree, and the standard CoC values for full frame, APS-C, Micro 4/3 and phone sensors.

Home › Guides › Circle of Confusion 
 Circle of Confusion Explained

 The one number hiding inside every depth of field calculation — and the reason calculators disagree with each other.

 What is the circle of confusion?

 A lens focuses only one plane perfectly. Everything else is a slightly out-of-focus circle of light on the sensor — the "circle of confusion." If that circle is small enough, your eye perceives the point as sharp. The circle of confusion (CoC) is the largest blur spot that still looks like a point in the final print.

 Two things decide it: how much you enlarge the image (a full-frame shot printed at 20×24 is enlarged ~8×; a phone shot at the same size is enlarged ~50×) and how close you view from . The classic assumption is an 8×10 print viewed from ~25 cm, which works out to a blur spot of about 1/1000 inch on the print.

 The standard values

 The most common convention is sensor diagonal ÷ 1500 (some use ÷ 1730 for an even stricter 8×10 standard). ShutterMath uses ÷ 1500 by default. That gives these values:

 Sensor format Dimensions (mm) Diagonal (mm) CoC ÷1500 (mm) 

 Full frame 36 × 24 43.3 0.029 

 APS-C (Sony / Nikon / Fujifilm) 23.5 × 15.6 28.2 0.019 

 APS-C (Canon) 22.3 × 14.9 26.8 0.018 

 Micro 4/3 17.3 × 13 21.6 0.014 

 1-inch 13.2 × 8.8 15.9 0.011 

 Phone main sensor (~1/1.28″) 9.8 × 7.3 12.2 0.008 

 Why do calculators give different answers?

 Different CoC standards. Diagonal ÷ 1500 vs ÷ 1730 vs a fixed 0.030 mm for everything vs pixel-based values. The stricter the CoC, the farther the hyperfocal distance and the smaller the depth of field.

 Different sensor dimensions. Some calculators use 36×24 for "full frame" regardless of the camera; exact values (35.9×23.9 for many Nikons) shift results a little.

 Formula variants. Older calculators omit the "+ f" term in the hyperfocal formula — negligible for wide lenses, a few percent for telephotos.

 Should you use a stricter CoC?

 If you pixel-peep at 100%, or print very large, the classic CoC is too generous. A common stricter choice is diagonal ÷ 2000 (full frame ≈ 0.022 mm). Because H = f²/(N·c), making the CoC one-third smaller makes the hyperfocal distance one-third larger and depth of field roughly one-third smaller. Our depth of field calculator lets you override the CoC — start with ÷2000 if you inspect images closely.

 Circle of confusion FAQ

 Does my camera's pixel size set the circle of confusion? Not directly. CoC is about perceived sharpness in the final image, not pixel size. Pixel-based "CoC" values are sometimes used for astrophotography (where a star should ideally land within one pixel), but for general photography the viewing-standard CoC is the right tool.

 What CoC does dofmaster or my camera's DoF preview use? Most classic calculators use diagonal ÷ 1500 (dofmaster lists ~0.029-0.030 mm for full frame). In-camera DoF previews use the lens's actual aperture and the sensor, but the on-screen preview is too small to judge precisely — calculators are more reliable for planning.

 Is a smaller CoC always more accurate? No — it's a threshold, not a measurement. A "stricter" CoC is more conservative (less of the image counts as sharp). Pick the standard that matches how you view: ÷1500 for normal prints, ÷2000 for pixel-peeping and large prints.

TITLE: Crop Factor Explained — Full Frame, APS-C & M4/3 | ShutterMath
SUMMARY: What crop factor really means: focal length and aperture equivalence computed for full frame, APS-C, Micro 4/3 and phone cameras — and why exposure doesn't change.

Home › Guides › Crop Factor Explained: Full Frame, APS-C & M4/3 Equivalents | ShutterMath 
 Crop Factor Explained: Full Frame, APS-C & M4/3 Equivalents | ShutterMath

 What crop factor really means: focal length and aperture equivalence computed for full frame, APS-C, Micro 4/3 and phone cameras — and why exposure doesn't change.

 Crop factor is the diagonal of a full-frame sensor (43.27 mm) divided by your sensor's diagonal. It answers one question: how does my lens frame and blur compared with the same lens on full frame? 

 Real crop factors, computed from sensor dimensions

 Camera Sensor Crop factor 

 Sony A1 II 36.0 × 24.0 mm 1.00× 
 Sony A6700 23.5 × 15.6 mm 1.53× 
 Canon EOS R7 22.3 × 14.9 mm 1.61× 
 Fujifilm X-T5 23.5 × 15.6 mm 1.53× 
 OM System OM-1 II 17.4 × 13.0 mm 1.99× 
 iPhone 16 Pro 9.8 × 7.3 mm 3.54× 

 Focal length equivalence (same framing)

 A lens on a smaller sensor frames like a longer lens on full frame. To match full-frame framing, multiply the focal length by the crop factor:

 Lens Full frame APS-C 1.52× Canon APS-C 1.6× M4/3 2× Phone 3.6× 

 24 mm 24 mm 36 mm 38 mm 48 mm 86 mm 
 35 mm 35 mm 53 mm 56 mm 70 mm 126 mm 
 50 mm 50 mm 76 mm 80 mm 100 mm 180 mm 
 85 mm 85 mm 129 mm 136 mm 170 mm 306 mm 
 135 mm 135 mm 205 mm 216 mm 270 mm 486 mm 

 Aperture equivalence (same depth of field)

 To match full-frame depth of field and background blur, multiply the aperture too. 50 mm f/1.8 on APS-C behaves like 75 mm f/2.7 on full frame — same framing, same blur:

 On this camera Equivalent on APS-C (1.5×) Equivalent on full frame 

 50 mm f/1.8 75 mm f/2.7 100 mm f/3.6 
 35 mm f/1.4 52 mm f/2.1 70 mm f/2.8 
 85 mm f/1.2 128 mm f/1.8 170 mm f/2.4 

 Full-frame users need 2× the focal length of M4/3 users, but also 2× the f-number for the same look. Compute your exact rig in the free depth of field calculator or field of view calculator .

 Crop factor FAQ

 What is crop factor? Full-frame diagonal (43.27 mm) ÷ your sensor diagonal. APS-C ≈ 1.5×, Canon APS-C ≈ 1.6×, Micro 4/3 = 2×.

 Does crop factor change exposure? No — never. Same aperture, shutter and ISO = same exposure on any format. Crop factor only changes framing and depth of field.

 Do lenses change focal length on crop sensors? No. A 50 mm lens is always 50 mm. It just frames like a 75 mm would on full frame.

SOURCE: https://shuttermath.com/pages/depth-of-field-astro.html
TITLE: Astrophotography Focus &amp; Depth of Field | ShutterMath
SUMMARY: Astrophotography focusing and DoF: why you focus at infinity (not the lens mark), the f-ratio trade-off for Milky Way shots, and the 500/NPF star-exposure rules.

Home › Guides › Astro Focus & DoF 
 Astrophotography Focus & Depth of Field

 Stars are at infinity — so astro DoF is less about "how much is sharp" and more about two numbers: nailing infinity focus, and how long you can expose before stars trail.

 Focusing at infinity, properly

 The lens infinity mark is a lie — most lenses overshoot infinity (they're built to focus slightly past it for thermal drift), so trusting the mark gives you slightly soft stars. Do this instead:

 Manual focus + live view at 10× on the brightest star you can find.

 Turn the focus ring until the star is the smallest, tightest point — not a disk with a halo.

 Focus-peaking (red highlight) makes this easy on mirrorless; tape the ring afterward if it drifts.

 For lenses with no stars visible (city glow), focus on the moon, a distant light, or use the lens's hard infinity stop then back off 1–2 mm of ring travel.

 A subtle point: a wide-angle at f/2.8 focused at 25 m instead of infinity still looks sharp because the hyperfocal distance is ~7 m — but a 135 mm lens at f/2 focused 1 m off infinity is visibly soft. Check your hyperfocal to know how much forgiveness you have.

 The f-ratio trade-off (Milky Way)

 Astro landscapes run the classic DoF trade-off against light collection:

 Aperture DoF at 24 mm, 5 m focus (FF) Astro verdict 

 f/1.4 ~4.0 m Maximum light, foreground risk — focus-stack foreground + sky 

 f/2 ~6.6 m The classic Milky Way choice 

 f/2.8 ~13.5 m Forgiving, still fast; hyperfocal ≈ 7 m 

 f/4 ~620 m (≈ ∞) Half the light of f/2 — needs ISO or stacking 

 The pro workflow: shoot the sky at f/1.8–f/2.8 focused at infinity, then shoot a foreground frame focused at 3–5 m and blend — you get maximum star light and a sharp foreground. That's DoF math applied to astro.

 How long before stars trail?

 Stars move ~15°/hour. The maximum exposure before visible trails depends on your lens and sensor:

 500 rule: 500 ÷ (focal × crop) — fine for old sensors, trails on 24 MP+.

 300 rule: 300 ÷ (focal × crop) — safer on modern high-res bodies.

 NPF rule: (35·N + 30·p) ÷ focal equiv — accounts for pixel size and aperture; the accurate choice.

 Example: 24 mm on a full-frame 45 MP camera (4.4 µm pixels) at f/2.8 → NPF ≈ (35×2.8 + 30×4.4) ÷ 24 = 9.6 s , vs the 500 rule's optimistic 20.8 s. Get your exact numbers in the star trails calculator .

 Astro focus FAQ

 Should I use autofocus at night? AF usually fails on stars (too little contrast). Focus manually with live-view magnification; some newer cameras have a "star AF" mode that works — worth testing, but manual is the reliable default.

 Why do my stars look like donuts? That's usually focus slightly off (the classic halo) or coma in the lens corners. Fix focus first; if corners still show it, stop down one stop and re-check.

 Do I need a star tracker? Not for wide-field Milky Way (the 500/NPF times are enough). For deep-sky through a telescope — yes, tracking is required, and then the exposure-time question becomes about noise, not trails.

SOURCE: https://shuttermath.com/pages/depth-of-field-landscape.html
TITLE: Depth of Field for Landscape Photography | ShutterMath
SUMMARY: Depth of field for landscape photography: hyperfocal focusing, the f-stop sweet spot (f/8-f/11), focus stacking, and the real numbers for common wide-angle.

Home › Guides › Landscape DoF 
 Depth of Field for Landscape Photography

 Landscape is the one genre where you usually want maximum depth of field. Here's the math that gets you there without guessing.

 The classic answer: hyperfocal focusing

 Focus at the hyperfocal distance and everything from half of it to infinity is acceptably sharp. For a 24 mm lens at f/8 on full frame (CoC 0.029 mm):

 Hyperfocal distance: 2.5 m — focus at ~2.5 m

 Sharp from 1.25 m to infinity 

 Stop down to f/11 and the hyperfocal distance drops to 1.84 m (sharp from 0.92 m). On APS-C the same lens at f/8 gives a hyperfocal distance of ~1.7 m — even easier. The full pre-computed table is in the hyperfocal distance chart , and the exact value for your camera is one click away in the hyperfocal calculator .

 The f-stop sweet spot

 Stopping down increases depth of field, but diffraction softens detail. The practical sweet spot:

 Format Sweet spot Diffraction visible beyond 

 Full frame f/8 – f/11 ~f/16 (avoid f/22 unless necessary) 

 APS-C f/5.6 – f/8 ~f/11 

 Micro 4/3 f/4 – f/5.6 ~f/8 

 Phone f/1.8 – f/2.8 (fixed) n/a — diffraction-free zone 

 If f/8 on your format doesn't give enough depth of field, don't chase f/22 — use focus stacking instead (below).

 When hyperfocal isn't enough

 Two situations break the hyperfocal approach:

 A very close foreground (a rock or flower 0.3 m from the lens) — even f/11 can't hold it and the horizon together. Set focus on the foreground and let the background blur, or…

 Focus stacking : shoot a series focused from near to far (typically 3–7 frames at f/8, moving the focus point ~⅓ of the DoF depth between shots) and blend in post. This gives f/8 sharpness at f/22 depth — the standard approach for pro landscape work.

 Practical workflow

 Compose, then pick your aperture: f/8 on full frame, f/5.6–f/8 on APS-C .

 Look up the hyperfocal distance (chart or calculator ) and set manual focus there.

 If a foreground element sits closer than half the hyperfocal distance, decide: foreground-focused shot, or a focus stack.

 Shoot, then check at 100%: if the nearest element is soft, focus nearer and reshoot — better than "fixing in post".

 Landscape DoF FAQ

 Should I focus at infinity instead of hyperfocal? Only if the scene is entirely distant (mountains across a valley). Focusing at infinity wastes the depth of field in front of you — hyperfocal gives you sharp foregrounds for free.

 Is the hyperfocal distance accurate on modern lenses? Most mirrorless lenses no longer print a distance scale, so set focus by looking at the lens-distance readout, using focus peaking, or by focusing on an object at the computed distance. The math is exact; your focus mechanism is the variable.

 Do I need a tripod for hyperfocal landscape shots? For maximum sharpness, yes — it lets you use the sweet-spot aperture without raising ISO, and it's essential for focus stacking. A tripod plus 2-second timer (or remote) removes mirror/camera-shake variables entirely.


------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SOURCE: https://shuttermath.com/pages/depth-of-field-macro.html
TITLE: Depth of Field for Macro Photography | ShutterMath
SUMMARY: Macro depth of field explained: why DoF shrinks with magnification, effective aperture, and the focus-stacking workflow that gets whole subjects sharp at 1:1 and.

Home › Guides › Macro DoF 
 Depth of Field for Macro Photography

 Macro is where depth of field stops being "a couple of meters" and becomes fractions of a millimeter. The math is different, the tools are different, and the workflow is focus stacking.

 The magnification problem

 At macro distances, depth of field follows DoF ≈ 2·N·c·(m+1)/m² , where m is magnification (1:1 = 1.0). The m² term is the killer — each doubling of magnification quarters the depth of field:

 Magnification DoF at f/8 (full frame) Effective aperture 

 1:4 (0.25×) ~9.3 mm f/10 

 1:2 (0.5×) ~2.8 mm f/12 

 1:1 (1.0×) ~0.93 mm f/16 

 2:1 (2.0×) ~0.35 mm f/24 

 3:1 (3.0×) ~0.21 mm f/32 

 An insect's eye sits maybe 1–2 mm from its wing — a 1:1 shot at f/8 can't hold both. And the effective aperture column shows the second problem: at 1:1, f/8 set is f/16 effective, losing two stops of light and gaining diffraction. Your exact numbers are in the macro DoF calculator .

 Why stopping down fails

 At 1:1, going from f/8 to f/16 doubles the DoF (0.93 → 1.86 mm) but the effective aperture hits f/32 — where diffraction has already softened everything to a similar blur as the DoF gain. The image looks "sharp" nowhere. This is why pro macro is done at f/5.6–f/11 with stacking, not f/32 single shots.

 The focus-stacking workflow

 Rig it: camera on a rail (or tripod with a focusing rail); subject still. Focus ring moves the lens, the rail moves the camera — for 1:1+ use the rail.

 Shoot wide-ish: f/5.6–f/11 (f/8 typical) to minimize diffraction while keeping a usable step size.

 Step by 80% of the DoF: the calculator's stacking step output is exactly this — move focus that far between frames. Overlap 20–30% so the stacking software has matching detail.

 Merge: Helicon Focus or Photoshop (Edit → Auto-Blend Layers). Review edges for halos; if present, use a smaller step.

 A 3 mm-deep subject at 1:1 with ~0.9 mm DoF needs roughly 4–6 frames . Live subjects (breathing, swaying) force a compromise: wider aperture, faster shutter, flash, and a smaller stack.

 Lighting and exposure at high magnification

 Effective aperture light loss: your camera meters through the lens so exposure is usually right — but manual flash math must add the stops (at 1:1, add 2 stops).

 Diffusion beats power: a diffused flash near the lens (ring or twin-flash) gives the short, motion-freezing light macro needs; continuous light means slower shutter and more shake.

 Focus at working aperture: focus wide open to see, stop down to shoot, or use focus peaking if available.

 Macro DoF FAQ

 Do I need a macro lens for focus stacking? No — extension tubes, close-up filters, or reversing rings on a normal lens all work. What matters is controlled focus movement: a rail for 1:1+, or a lens with a smooth focus ring for lower magnifications.

 Why does my 100 mm macro show more DoF than a 60 mm at the same magnification? At the same magnification, focal length mostly cancels out of the macro DoF formula — the difference you see is usually working distance (100 mm lets you shoot from farther, which helps light and skittish subjects, not DoF).

 Can I stack handheld shots? Software can align handheld stacks, but success drops fast at 1:1 — the alignment quality suffers and steps become uneven. Tripod + rail until the subject forces you handheld, then burst-shoot and hope for 2–4 usable frames.


------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SOURCE: https://shuttermath.com/pages/depth-of-field-portrait.html
TITLE: Depth of Field for Portrait Photography | ShutterMath
SUMMARY: Portrait depth of field: how much background blur do you actually need, which lens/aperture/distance combos deliver it, and the real numbers for 50mm, 85mm and.

Home › Guides › Portrait DoF 
 Depth of Field for Portrait Photography

 Portraits are the opposite of landscapes: you want shallow depth of field, placed so the eyes are sharp and the rest falls away. The numbers make it predictable.

 How much DoF is actually right?

 The classic portrait target is both eyes sharp — about 3–8 cm of depth of field at the eyes for a head-and-shoulders shot. Much less and one eye blurs; much more and the background starts competing with the subject.

 Here's the real math (full frame, CoC 0.029 mm, subject at 2 m):

 Lens Aperture Total DoF at 2 m Result 

 50 mm f/1.8 ~16 cm Good — safe for head-and-shoulders 

 85 mm f/1.8 ~5.5 cm Classic — both eyes sharp, hair softens 

 85 mm f/2.8 ~9 cm Forgiving group/candid choice 

 135 mm f/2 ~2 cm Very thin — focus on the near eye, recompose 

 These come straight from the depth of field calculator — change the subject distance to 3 m and every number roughly doubles.

 The three levers (and their limits)

 Focal length: 85–135 mm compresses perspective and magnifies background blur. 50 mm needs to be close — which distorts features at very short distances.

 Aperture: f/1.2–f/2 gives the thinnest DoF but the thinnest margin for focus error — at f/1.2 a 2 cm shift in the subject's pose can move their eyes out of the sharp zone.

 Subject-to-background distance: the most underrated lever. Move the subject 2 m from the background and even f/4 produces creamy separation; with the subject against a wall, no lens can save it.

 Focus technique for thin DoF

 Focus on the near eye (single-point AF, eye-detection on mirrorless) — the near eye is what viewers lock onto.

 Shoot at the widest aperture that keeps both eyes sharp for the framing — check the DoF number, don't guess.

 Watch the ⅓–⅔ rule: about ⅓ of the DoF sits in front of the focus point, ⅔ behind — so focus slightly toward you if the far eye matters.

 If using a 135 mm at f/2, shoot a quick burst and pick the sharpest frame — a 2 cm DoF moves with the subject's sway.

 APS-C and Micro 4/3 portraits

 On APS-C, an 85 mm f/1.8 at 2 m gives ~4 cm of DoF — still perfect for portraits; the crop just changes your working distance for the same framing (step back to ~2.7 m for head-and-shoulders, which widens DoF to ~7 cm). On Micro 4/3, a 45 mm f/1.8 behaves like a 90 mm full-frame field of view with roughly the DoF of an f/3.6 full-frame lens — the format's famous "two-stop" penalty. Same framing, more DoF than full frame; you compensate with faster lenses or more background distance.

 Depth of Field Calculator
 Your exact near/far limits for any lens, distance, and camera.

 Keep the aperture you want and still get correct flash exposure.

 Why format changes the "look" of the same lens.

 Portrait DoF FAQ

 Why do my f/1.8 portraits have one eye sharp and the other soft? At typical 85 mm f/1.8 portrait distances your total DoF is only ~5 cm — less than the distance between a subject's eyes when they turn their head. Solution: stop to f/2.8 (DoF ~9 cm) or ask for a slight profile angle so both eyes are in the same plane.

 Does a 50 mm f/1.2 give the same blur as an 85 mm f/1.8? At the same subject framing and distance-to-background, no — background blur scales mostly with focal length and subject-to-background distance. The 85 mm compresses and blurs more, which is why it's the classic portrait focal length.

 Is background blur the same as depth of field? Related but not identical. DoF is the sharp zone in front of/behind the subject; background blur is how strongly a background beyond the DoF falls off. A long lens can have both shallow DoF and heavy background blur; a fast wide lens has shallow DoF but mild background blur.

SOURCE: https://shuttermath.com/pages/depth-of-field-real-estate.html
TITLE: Depth of Field for Real Estate Photography | ShutterMath
SUMMARY: Real estate photography depth of field: the f/8 sweet spot, focus at the right third point, and why interior sharpness from wall to wall is a solved math problem.

Home › Guides › Real Estate DoF 
 Depth of Field for Real Estate Photography

 Real estate is the opposite of portraits: you want everything sharp from the countertop to the back window. Good news — it's a solved math problem, and the answer is usually f/8.

 The f/8 rule, with math

 A 16 mm lens on full frame at f/8 has a hyperfocal distance of about 1.1 m — focus at 1.1 m and everything from 0.55 m to infinity is sharp. That covers an entire room. On APS-C, a 10–12 mm lens at f/8 is similar (~0.7–0.9 m hyperfocal). Get exact values in the hyperfocal calculator or the chart .

 Focal length (FF) Hyperfocal @ f/8 Sharp from 

 14 mm 0.86 m 0.43 m → ∞ 

 16 mm 1.13 m 0.56 m → ∞ 

 20 mm 1.75 m 0.88 m → ∞ 

 24 mm 2.52 m 1.26 m → ∞ 

 That's why f/8 is the real-estate default : f/5.6 risks a soft near edge, and f/11–f/16 buys almost nothing (the near limit barely moves) while adding diffraction. f/8 is the diffraction-free sweet spot with more than enough DoF.

 Where to focus

 The classic method: focus ⅓ into the room (not the back wall, not the floor). At hyperfocal it doesn't matter — focus at H and everything from H/2 to infinity is sharp. Practical workflow:

 Compose the room, set f/8, focus on a point about ⅓ of the way into the frame (a chair arm, the middle of a counter).

 If your lens has no distance scale (most mirrorless), focus-peak on something at the ⅓ point or use the hyperfocal number with the focus ring's readout.

 For large rooms or angled shots where the nearest element is closer than H/2, focus on the nearest element and stop to f/11 if needed — or take two focus-bracketed shots.

 Technique details that matter

 Tripod, always. At f/8 and ISO 100 you'll be at 1/4–1 s indoors — no handheld margin. Level the camera (bubble or electronic level) so verticals stay straight.

 HDR/Exposure blending: windows blow out at any single exposure. Shoot 3–5 brackets (±2 EV) and blend — the DoF math is identical for every frame, so brackets stack cleanly.

 Vertical framing for tight spaces (bathrooms): tilt shift? No — keep the camera level and stitch two vertical frames later. Tilting the camera up ruins verticals even if DoF still covers the room.

 Flash or ambient? HDR ambient is the norm; flash adds punch but complicates DoF (flash falloff needs higher ISO or more power, not aperture changes).
