 Real estate DoF FAQ

 Why does my real estate shot look sharp in the middle but soft at the edges? Lens field curvature or corner softness, not DoF — wide lenses are softest at the edges wide open. Stop to f/8–f/11 (where the lens is sharpest) and check if the corners recover; if not, it's lens quality, and no aperture change fixes it.

 Should I shoot f/11 to be safe? Only if the nearest element is inside H/2. On full frame with a 16 mm lens that means closer than ~0.55 m — rare in a composed room shot. f/11's diffraction starts to soften overall detail for zero practical DoF gain. Use f/8 and a correct focus point.

 Does a tilt-shift lens change the DoF math? Yes — tilt changes the plane of focus, so a tilted lens can have a "wedge" of sharpness covering a floor-to-ceiling scene at f/5.6 where a regular lens would need f/8+. The hyperfocal numbers here apply to regular (non-tilted) lenses.

SOURCE: https://shuttermath.com/pages/depth-of-field-sports.html
TITLE: Depth of Field for Sports &amp; Action Photography | ShutterMath
SUMMARY: Sports photography DoF and shutter strategy: freeze motion, track subjects, and keep the sharp zone where it matters — with real numbers for telephoto action.

Home › Guides › Sports DoF 
 Depth of Field for Sports & Action Photography

 Action photography fights two battles at once: shutter speed fast enough to freeze motion, and aperture wide enough for light — which leaves you with a very thin depth of field that's moving. Here's how to win both.

 The numbers you're fighting

 A 70–200 mm f/2.8 on full frame, subject at 20 m, shot at f/2.8:

 Focal length Aperture Total DoF @ 20 m Reality 

 70 mm f/2.8 ~2.1 m Forgiving — most of an athlete fits 

 135 mm f/2.8 ~0.57 m Eyes-to-knees tight; tracking must be good 

 200 mm f/2.8 ~0.26 m Sharp face, blurred everything else — focus must be nailed 

 200 mm f/5.6 ~0.52 m Double the DoF, one stop less light 

 At 200 mm, a runner moving toward you can shift 0.5 m between your focus lock and shutter — that's the entire DoF. Run your own numbers for your lens and distance.

 The shutter speed partner

 DoF decisions only matter if motion is frozen. From the shutter speed chart : 1/1000–1/2000 s for most sports, 1/2000+ for birds in flight and ball-in-frame moments. Sports shooters live in the exposure triangle: wide aperture for light, fast shutter for freeze, ISO as the balancing valve (modern bodies handle 3200–6400 well — see the exposure calculator ).

 Keeping the sharp zone on the subject

 Track with AF-C and your best eye/face detection — let the camera chase the eye, not the jersey.

 Prefocus at a known spot (goal line, finish line, hoop) and shoot when the action arrives — zero tracking risk, razor sharp.

 Anticipate the plane: subjects moving across the frame keep a constant distance (DoF stays put); subjects moving toward you blow through the DoF — that's when burst + tracking matters most.

 Stop down when you can: f/4 on a 200 mm gives ~0.37 m at 20 m and works in good light — a big margin gain for one stop of ISO.

 Panning: blur as a tool

 Sometimes you want the background blurred but the subject sharp: pan with the subject at 1/60–1/125 s. The DoF still applies (keep the subject in the sharp zone), but the background blur comes from motion, not aperture — so you can shoot f/5.6–f/8 for a wider safety margin.

 Sports DoF FAQ

 Why are my action shots sharp on the jersey but soft on the face? Thin DoF + tracking lag. At 200 mm f/2.8 the sharp zone can be ~25 cm — enough for a face, not a face + chest. Use eye-detection AF, shoot at the peak of the action, and consider f/4 for a bigger margin.

 Should I use back-button focus for sports? Many pros do — it separates focus from shutter so you can track continuously and shoot without refocusing. It's a habit change, but it removes the shutter-press refocus delay.

 Is a 2.8 zoom worth it over f/4 for indoor sports? Indoors, one stop is often the difference between ISO 6400 and 12800. If you shoot gyms and arenas, f/2.8 (or primes) is worth it; outdoors in daylight, f/4 zooms are lighter and equally sharp.

 How to read this table

 Rows are focus distances, columns are apertures. Each cell shows near limit – far limit (total depth of field in brackets). Focus at the distance, and everything between near and far is acceptably sharp at the standard circle of confusion (sensor diagonal ÷ 1500).

 Two patterns to notice: closing the aperture pushes the far limit out faster than the near limit moves (⅓ in front, ⅔ behind), and moving your focus distance further away multiplies the depth of field roughly with the square of distance.

 FAQ

 Are these tables exact for my lens? They use the standard formula H = f²/(N·c) + f with CoC = sensor diagonal ÷ 1500, which matches the classic published tables (dofmaster-style values). Real-world results vary slightly with lens breathing, focus accuracy, and your viewing standard — treat them as planning numbers, not promises.

 Why is the depth of field different on APS-C? Two reasons: the smaller sensor needs a shorter lens for the same framing (which we account for by using the same focal length — so on APS-C you're effectively seeing a tighter crop), and its circle of confusion is smaller, which shortens the near/far spread. For same-framing comparisons, mentally multiply the APS-C aperture by 1.5.

 3 m 2.92 m – 3.08 m (16 cm) 2.91 m – 3.10 m (19 cm) 2.88 m – 3.12 m (24 cm) 2.87 m – 3.14 m (27 cm) 2.82 m – 3.20 m (37 cm) 2.76 m – 3.29 m (54 cm) 2.67 m – 3.42 m (76 cm) 2.55 m – 3.65 m (1.10 m)

 10 m 9.18 m – 11 m (1.81 m) 9.05 m – 11 m (2.12 m) 8.81 m – 12 m (2.74 m) 8.70 m – 12 m (3.06 m) 8.27 m – 13 m (4.38 m) 7.70 m – 14 m (6.56 m) 7.05 m – 17 m (10 m) 6.26 m – 25 m (19 m) 

 How to read this table

 Rows are focus distances, columns are apertures. Each cell shows near limit – far limit (total depth of field in brackets). Focus at the distance, and everything between near and far is acceptably sharp at the standard circle of confusion (sensor diagonal ÷ 1500).

 Two patterns to notice: closing the aperture pushes the far limit out faster than the near limit moves (⅓ in front, ⅔ behind), and moving your focus distance further away multiplies the depth of field roughly with the square of distance.

 FAQ

 Are these tables exact for my lens? They use the standard formula H = f²/(N·c) + f with CoC = sensor diagonal ÷ 1500, which matches the classic published tables (dofmaster-style values). Real-world results vary slightly with lens breathing, focus accuracy, and your viewing standard — treat them as planning numbers, not promises.

 Why is the depth of field different on APS-C? Two reasons: the smaller sensor needs a shorter lens for the same framing (which we account for by using the same focal length — so on APS-C you're effectively seeing a tighter crop), and its circle of confusion is smaller, which shortens the near/far spread. For same-framing comparisons, mentally multiply the APS-C aperture by 1.5.

SOURCE: https://shuttermath.com/pages/exposure-triangle.html
TITLE: Exposure Triangle Explained | ShutterMath
SUMMARY: The exposure triangle explained with real numbers: what aperture, shutter speed and ISO each do, how they trade off to keep the same exposure, and which to.

Home › Guides › Exposure Triangle 
 Exposure Triangle Explained

 Three controls, one result: the amount of light that reaches your sensor. Here's what each one does, how they trade off, and which to change first — with numbers you can verify in the exposure equivalence calculator .

 The three corners

 Control What it changes Cost of overdoing it One stop = 

 Aperture (f/) Amount of light + depth of field Narrow apertures → diffraction softness f/2.8 → f/4 → f/5.6 → f/8… (each halves the light) 

 Shutter speed (s) Amount of light + motion blur Slow speeds → camera shake and subject blur 1/500 → 1/250 → 1/125 → 1/60… (each doubles the light) 

 ISO Amplification of the captured light High ISO → visible noise 100 → 200 → 400 → 800 (each doubles sensitivity) 

 The trade-off, with real numbers

 Say your meter says f/4 · 1/250 s · ISO 100 . That's an exposure value of EV100 = 12. Every combination below captures the same amount of light :

 Aperture Shutter ISO Result 

 f/4 1/250 s 100 Starting point — balanced 

 f/2.8 1/500 s 100 Shallower DoF, freezes motion 

 f/5.6 1/125 s 100 More DoF, risk of blur 

 f/4 1/500 s 200 Faster shutter, ISO doubles 

 f/8 1/60 s 100 Maximum DoF, needs steady camera 

 Every row is identically bright. The only differences are aesthetic : depth of field, motion blur, and noise. That's why "correct exposure" is a creative choice, not a number.

 Which corner to change first (priority order)

 Shutter speed first — set the slowest speed that still freezes your subject (1/focal length handheld, or the subject chart ). Motion blur is the one mistake you can't fix.

 Aperture second — dial the depth of field your shot needs (f/1.8 portrait vs f/8 landscape), then…

 ISO last — raise ISO only to make up the remaining difference. Modern cameras are clean up to ISO 1600–3200; noise beats blur.

 Common exposure mistakes

 "I'll fix it in post." Raising exposure in editing amplifies noise and clips highlights. Better to expose right (or deliberately overexpose by ⅓–⅔ stop for shadows, then recover — the "expose to the right" technique).

 Chasing shallow DoF everywhere. f/1.2 portraits with drifting focus are soft; the portrait guide shows when to stop down.

 ISO fear. On a modern camera, ISO 3200 in low light is usually better than a 1/15 s blurry shot at ISO 100.

 Related tools & guides

 Exposure Equivalence Calculator
 Generate every equivalent exposure for your settings.
 Open → 
 Shutter Speed Chart
 The right shutter for every subject.
 Read → 
 Depth of Field Calculator

 Open → 

 Exposure triangle FAQ

 Does ISO really belong in the "exposure" triangle? Strictly, exposure is light only (aperture × shutter). ISO is amplification applied after capture. But in practice the three work together to set final brightness, so the triangle is the useful mental model — with the caveat that ISO doesn't add light, it adds noise.

 What is "stopping down" and "opening up"? One stop = doubling or halving the light. Opening up (wider aperture, slower shutter, higher ISO) doubles light; stopping down halves it. The exposure equivalence calculator does the bookkeeping for you.

 Why do my photos look different at the same exposure? Because exposure isn't the whole picture — the character changes with settings: bokeh from aperture, blur from shutter, grain from ISO. Same brightness, different image. That's exactly why the triangle matters.

TITLE: Exposure Value (EV) Chart — Reference for Any Light | ShutterMath
SUMMARY: Printable exposure value chart: EV -6 to +17 with scene examples, the shutter speed at f/1.0, and the aperture needed for 1/125 s — all at ISO 100.

Home › Guides › Exposure Value (EV) Chart 
 Exposure Value (EV) Chart

 Printable exposure value chart: EV -6 to +17 with scene examples, the shutter speed at f/1.0, and the aperture needed for 1/125 s — all at ISO 100.

 Exposure value (EV) is a single number that describes how bright a scene is. The formula, at ISO 100, is EV = log₂(N²/t) , where N is the f-number and t the shutter time in seconds. Each step of +1 EV doubles the light. Every row below is computed from that formula — nothing approximate.

 EV reference table (ISO 100)

 EV Typical scene (approx.) Shutter at f/1.0 Aperture for 1/125 s 

 -6 Starlit night sky 64 s — 

 -5 Aurora / deep twilight 32 s — 

 -4 Night landscape, faint aurora 16 s — 

 -3 Night under bright moonlight 8 s — 

 -2 Full-moon night landscape 4 s — 

 -1 Late dusk, lit skyline 2 s — 

 0 Very dim interior / candlelight at distance 1 s — 

 1 Candlelit close-up 1/2 s — 

 2 Dim indoor lighting 1/4 s — 

 3 City night, street-lit 1/8 s — 

 4 Home interiors at night 1/16 s — 

 5 Bright indoor / dusk sports 1/32 s — 

 6 Overcast evening / office light 1/64 s — 

 7 Open shade, late sun 1/128 s f/1.0 

 8 Overcast day / bright shade 1/256 s f/1.4 

 9 Bright overcast 1/512 s f/2.0 

 10 Hazy sun 1/1024 s f/2.9 

 11 Light clouds, sunlight 1/2048 s f/4.0 

 12 Bright daylight 1/4096 s f/5.7 

 13 Sunny, light haze 1/8192 s f/8.1 

 14 Full sun, light sand or snow 1/16384 s f/11.4 

 15 Bright sun (sunny 16) 1/32768 s f/16.2 

 16 Snow or beach in full sun 1/65536 s f/22.9 

 17 Very bright snow or water 1/131072 s — 

 How to use it

 Meter the scene (your camera shows EV in some modes, or estimate from the table), then pick any aperture/shutter pair on the same EV line. Want the exact equivalents — including ISO changes? Use the free exposure calculator , which does this for your camera in one click.

 EV FAQ

 What is exposure value (EV)? EV = log₂(N²/t) at ISO 100 — one number that encodes aperture and shutter together. Brighter scene = higher EV.

 Why is EV measured at ISO 100? Convention. The same scene has the same EV regardless of ISO; your ISO choice just changes which aperture/shutter pairs keep the exposure correct.

 What is sunny 16? In bright sun at f/16, the correct shutter is 1/ISO seconds — that's EV 15 at ISO 100. The chart shows EV 15 ↔ f/16 at 1/125 s for ISO 100.

SOURCE: https://shuttermath.com/pages/focal-length-explained.html
TITLE: Focal Length Explained: 24mm to 200mm | ShutterMath
SUMMARY: Focal length explained: angles of view for 14–200 mm, wide vs normal vs telephoto, what 24/35/50/85 mm are each for, and why perspective comes from distance, not.

Home › Guides › Focal Length Explained 
 Focal Length Explained

 Angles of view for 14–200 mm, what wide/normal/telephoto each do, and why perspective comes from where you stand — not your lens.

 Focal length is the distance in millimetres between the lens's optical center and the sensor when focused at infinity. It sets one thing: angle of view . Short focal lengths show a wide scene; long ones magnify a narrow slice. Everything else about lens choice follows from that.

 Angle of view by focal length (full frame)

 Focal length Horizontal angle of view Typical use 

 14 mm 104.3° Ultra-wide: architecture, astro, dramatic interiors 

 20 mm 84.0° Wide: landscape, real estate, tight interiors 

 24 mm 73.7° Wide: landscape, street, vlogging 

 28 mm 65.5° Wide-normal: documentary, travel 

 35 mm 54.4° Normal-wide: street, environmental portraits, reportage 

 50 mm 39.6° Normal: the natural look, portraits, everything 

 85 mm 23.9° Short tele: classic portrait length, compression 

 100 mm 20.4° Tele: portraits, macro, headshots 

 135 mm 15.2° Tele: headshots, sports, isolation 

 200 mm 10.3° Tele: wildlife, sports, compression 

 Angles computed with the standard formula AOV = 2·arctan(sensor width / (2·focal length)). On APS-C, Micro 4/3 or phones, the same lens frames differently — see the crop factor guide .

 What each focal length is for

 Ultra-wide (14–24 mm): space, drama, context. Great for real estate and astro, but easy to make empty scenes look empty.

 Wide (24–35 mm): the travel/street range. Fits more story in frame while keeping a natural look.

 Normal (50 mm): what your eye roughly sees. Unflattering to features up close, flattering at distance — the classic all-rounder.

 Short tele (85–135 mm): the portrait range. Compresses features, flatters faces, and backgrounds blur beautifully.

 Tele (135 mm+): reach and isolation for wildlife, sports, and candid shots.

 The perspective myth

 A wide lens doesn't "exaggerate" and a telephoto doesn't "compress" — distance does both . Photograph a face at 24 mm from 30 cm and at 135 mm from 3 m, then crop the wide shot to match the telephoto: the perspective is identical. Lenses only change what fits in the frame; where you stand changes the picture.

 Focal length FAQ

 What does focal length mean? The mm distance from lens to sensor at infinity focus — it sets angle of view: shorter = wider, longer = more magnified.

 What is a normal lens? About 50 mm on full frame, 35 mm on APS-C — the natural, unexaggerated look.

 Does focal length change perspective? No. Distance changes perspective. Focal length only changes how much fits in the frame.

 What is 35 mm equivalent? Your lens's focal length on full frame, given the same field of view: multiply by your sensor's crop factor .

 💡 Reading the chart: pick your sensor column, your focal length row, and your aperture — the number is the hyperfocal distance in metres. Focus your lens there (manual focus + distance scale) and everything from half that distance to infinity is sharp.

 Hyperfocal distance FAQ

 Are these distances exact? They use the standard circle-of-confusion convention (sensor diagonal ÷ 1500) and the formula H = f²/(N·c) + f, rounded to two decimal places. On very high-resolution sensors a stricter CoC pushes the numbers ~33% farther.

 Why is hyperfocal distance shorter on smaller sensors? Smaller sensors have smaller circles of confusion (the blur threshold scales with the sensor), and for the same framing they use shorter focal lengths. Both effects pull the hyperfocal distance closer — one reason phone cameras are sharp from near to far.

SOURCE: https://shuttermath.com/pages/long-exposure.html
TITLE: Long Exposure Photography — Settings & ND | ShutterMath
SUMMARY: Long exposure photography settings: the exact workflow from meter to shutter release, which ND filter strength for which effect, and the exposure math that makes.

Home › Guides › Long Exposure 
 Long Exposure Photography — Settings & Workflow

 Silky waterfalls, empty streets, streaking car lights: all the same trick — keep the shutter open long enough that motion becomes blur. Here's the exact workflow, with the math at each step.

 The workflow, step by step

 Compose and focus — focus, then switch to manual. Autofocus at f/11 in the dark will hunt.

 Set aperture + ISO: f/8–f/11 for depth of field (see landscape DoF ), ISO 100 always.

 Meter without the filter — note the shutter speed your meter wants (e.g. 1/60 s at f/11).

 Decide your target time — how blurred do you want the motion?

 Find the ND stops: stops = log₂(target ÷ base). 1/60 s → 15 s needs log₂(900) ≈ 9.8 stops → an ND1000 (10 stops) gets you to ~17 s.

 Mount the filter, set bulb (or the computed speed), release — remote release or 2-second timer, never your finger.

 Check the histogram — if highlights clip, add a stop of ND or shorten; the first frame is a test frame.

 Which effect needs which exposure

 Effect Typical time ND needed (from 1/60 s base) Notes 

 Slight motion in water ¼ – 1 s ND8–ND16 (3–4 stops) Mist starts; keep rocks crisp 

 Silky waterfall 2 – 8 s ND64–ND1000 (6–10 stops) The classic look 

 Empty streets / crowds gone 15 – 60 s ND1000+ (10+ stops) People vanish; car lights streak 

 Light trails 10 – 30 s ND1000 (10 stops) Night — often no ND needed 

 Clouds streaking 1 – 5 min ND1000+ stacked Check for sensor hotspots 

 Run your own numbers with the ND filter calculator or read straight off the long exposure chart .

 The three mistakes that ruin long exposures

 Shooting at f/22 "for sharpness." Diffraction beats the DoF gain; f/8–f/11 is sharper. If you need more depth, focus-stack.

 Trusting the filter's rated density. Budget NDs can be off by a third of a stop — meter through the filter when possible, or bracket.

 Camera shake you can't see. Tripod + remote + mirror lockup (DSLRs) + switch off image stabilization on the tripod (it can hunt and add micro-shake).

 Long exposure math, plainly

 Each ND stop doubles the shutter time: 1/60 → 1/30 → 1/15 → 1/8 → ¼ → ½ → 1 s → 2 s → 4 s → 8 s → 16 s → 32 s. Ten stops (ND1000) turns 1/60 s into ~17 s. That's the entire calculation — the calculator and chart just do it for you, including the awkward fractions.

 ND Filter Calculator
 Exact shutter for any filter and base exposure.
 Open → 
 ND Filter Long Exposure Chart
 The full pre-computed table, printable.

 Shutter Speed Chart

 Long exposure FAQ

 Do I need a 10-stop ND, or is 6 enough? It depends on the effect. ND64 (6 stops) takes 1/60 s to ~1 s — fine for misty water. ND1000 (10 stops) reaches 15–30 s — the crowd-removing, cloud-streaking territory. Most photographers own both; a variable ND covers the middle.

 Why is my long exposure purple or green? Color cast from the ND filter — cheap filters shift toward magenta/green. Fix in post with a white-balance eyedropper on a neutral area, or buy higher-quality glass. Stacking two cheap filters worsens the cast.

 Can I do long exposures on a phone? Modern phones have built-in long exposure / light-trail modes that stack frames instead of opening the shutter — different technique, same look. The composition and subject advice here applies identically.

SOURCE: https://shuttermath.com/pages/low-light.html
TITLE: Low Light Photography — Noise vs Blur Settings | ShutterMath
SUMMARY: Low light photography settings: the noise-vs-blur trade-off, which ISO to use, real EV numbers for night scenes, and when a tripod beats every sensor.

Home › Guides › Low Light 
 Low Light Photography — Noise vs Blur

 Every low-light shot is a trade: raise ISO and get noise, slow the shutter and get blur, open the aperture and lose depth of field. Here's how to pick the least-bad option — with the numbers.

 How dark is "low light"? (EV reality check)

 Exposure value (EV100) is the shorthand. The exposure calculator computes it; here's the map:

 EV100 Scene Handheld settings (f/1.8, ISO 3200) 

 15 Bright sun 1/8000 s — you'll never see this 

 10 Overcast day 1/250 s 

 7 Sunset / bright interior 1/30 s — edge of handheld 

 5 City night / lit street 1/8 s — needs a tripod or IBIS 

 3 Home interior, evening 1/2 s — tripod territory 

 0 Full moon night landscape 8 s — tripod, or see astro 

 -3 Starlight only 60 s+ — astrophotography 

 The decision order

 Is the camera still? Tripod → use base ISO and whatever shutter/aperture you like; noise becomes irrelevant. This is the single biggest low-light upgrade, and it's free.

 Handheld? Set the slowest safe shutter first (1/focal length, or 2–4 stops slower with stabilization — see the shutter speed chart ). Blur from camera shake is unrecoverable; noise is at least manageable.

 Open the aperture as far as your depth of field allows (f/1.8 portrait vs f/5.6 group shot — the DoF calculator shows the cost).

 Then raise ISO last , until the meter is happy. Modern full-frame bodies are clean to 6400; APS-C to ~3200; phones fake it with multi-frame stacking.

 ISO: the honest guide

 Base ISO (100–200): always when on a tripod.

 ISO 800–1600: invisible on most cameras. Free light for handheld shots.

 ISO 3200–6400: fine for full frame and good APS-C; noise is visible but printable. Better than a blurry ISO 400 shot. 

 ISO 12800+: emergency only — or embrace the grain; monochrome conversion hides it beautifully.

 Two practical low-light recipes

 Situation Settings Why 

 Night street, handheld f/2.8 · 1/60 s · ISO 3200 Fast enough to freeze people; IBIS helps at 1/60 

 Night street, tripod f/8 · 8 s · ISO 100 Maximum DoF, zero noise; car lights streak 

 Indoor party, handheld f/1.8 · 1/125 s · ISO 1600–3200 Thin DoF accepted; motion frozen 

 Milky Way (wide) f/2 · 10–15 s · ISO 3200 See the star trails calculator for the max time

 Low light FAQ

 Is high ISO noise or underexposure noise? Both. Noise is mostly set by how little light the sensor captures (underexposure), then amplified by ISO. "Expose to the right" — brighten the exposure in camera (via ISO or shutter) to keep signal high, then recover in post. Noise reduction software works best on properly exposed frames.

 Does image stabilization help moving subjects? No — IBIS/lens IS only cancels your shake, not subject motion. A person walking needs 1/60–1/125 regardless of stabilization. Stabilization buys handheld capability for static subjects (buildings, night streets).

 Why does my phone take better night shots than my camera? Phones stack many short exposures (computational photography) to cancel noise, then sharpen with AI. Your camera can do the same: bracket 5–10 shots on a tripod and average them in post — the "poor man's astro" technique that works for night cityscapes too.

 Privacy Policy

 Last updated: August 3, 2026

 1. Who we are

 ShutterMath ("we", "us") is an independent website providing free photography calculators. This policy explains what data we process and why. Contact: hello@shuttermath.com .

 2. Data we process

 a. Calculator inputs and saved setups

 Everything you type into a calculator is processed entirely in your browser . "Saved setups" are stored in your browser's local storage and never transmitted to us. We cannot see your camera, lens, or distance values.

 b. Privacy-friendly analytics

 We use lightweight, privacy-respecting analytics (no advertising cookies, no cross-site tracking, no personal identifiers such as IPs retained in identifiable form) to understand which tools and pages are useful. Analytics data is aggregate: page views, rough country, device type, referrer.

 c. Advertising (only with your consent)

 We may display ads served by Google AdSense only after you click "Accept" on the consent banner (or where you are not in the EEA/UK and no consent is required by law). If you consent, Google and its partners may use cookies to personalize ads, measure ad performance, and deliver relevant advertising, as described in Google's Privacy & Terms. You can withdraw consent at any time by clearing your browser storage for this site.

 Third-party vendor disclosure: Third-party vendors, including Google, use cookies to serve ads based on a user's prior visits to this website or other websites. Users may opt out of personalised advertising by visiting Google Ads Settings . Users may also opt out of some third-party vendors' use of cookies for personalised advertising by visiting www.aboutads.info (the Digital Advertising Alliance opt-out page) or the Network Advertising Initiative opt-out page . To opt out of Google Analytics Advertising Features, visit Google Analytics Opt-out .

 For visitors in the EEA/UK, we use a Google-certified consent management platform to obtain and record your choices under GDPR and the ePrivacy Directive before any advertising or personalization cookies load.

 Under GDPR you may request access, rectification, erasure, restriction, or portability of personal data, and withdraw consent at any time. You may also lodge a complaint with your supervisory authority.

SOURCE: https://shuttermath.com/pages/sharpest-aperture.html
TITLE: Sharpest Aperture — Diffraction Explained | ShutterMath
SUMMARY: Every lens has a sweet spot. Diffraction-limited apertures computed for real cameras: where the Airy disk meets your sensor's pixel pitch — and the practical.

Home › Guides › Sharpest Aperture for Every Camera 
 Sharpest Aperture for Every Camera

 Every lens has a sweet spot. Diffraction-limited apertures computed for real cameras: where the Airy disk meets your sensor's pixel pitch — and the practical f-stops to use.

 Every lens has a sharpness sweet spot. Wide open, optical aberrations soften the edges; stop down and they improve — but eventually diffraction takes over and the image softens again. The balance point is different for every camera, and it's computable.

 The Airy disk: where softness comes from

 Light passing through a circular aperture doesn't focus to a point — it spreads into a blur disc called the Airy disk, diameter 2.44 × λ × N (λ ≈ 0.55 µm for green light). When that disk grows larger than your sensor's pixels, diffraction is visible at 100%:

 Aperture Airy disk diameter 

 f/1.4 1.9 µm 
 f/2 2.7 µm 
 f/2.8 3.8 µm 
 f/4 5.4 µm 
 f/5.6 7.5 µm 
 f/8 10.7 µm 
 f/11 14.8 µm 
 f/16 21.5 µm 
 f/22 29.5 µm 

 Diffraction-limited aperture for real cameras

 Pixels are smaller on high-resolution sensors, so they hit the diffraction wall sooner. The table shows each camera's pixel pitch and the f-stop where the Airy disk reaches about two pixels — the practical point of visible softening:

 Camera Sensor Pixel pitch Diffraction-limited ≈ 

 Sony A1 II 36.0 × 24.0 mm 4.17 µm ≈ f/8 
 Sony A7 IV 36.0 × 24.0 mm 5.14 µm ≈ f/8 
 Canon EOS R5 II 36.0 × 24.0 mm 4.39 µm ≈ f/8 
 Fujifilm X-T5 23.5 × 15.6 mm 3.03 µm ≈ f/5.6 
 OM System OM-1 II 17.4 × 13.0 mm 3.35 µm ≈ f/5.6 
 iPhone 16 Pro 9.8 × 7.3 mm 1.21 µm ≈ f/2 

 Practical sweet spots

 Portraits: f/1.8–f/2.8 — sharpness isn't the point; blur is.

 Landscapes (tripod): f/8–f/11 — f/8 is the safe sweet spot, f/11 for extra DoF.

 Real estate / interiors: f/8 — enough depth, still pixel-sharp.

 Macro: stop down freely; focus stacking beats diffraction.

 Want the numbers for your exact camera and lens? The free depth of field calculator pairs any body in the database with any aperture.

 Related tools & guides

 Depth of Field Calculator
 DoF and hyperfocal for your exact sensor.
 Open → 
 Camera Sensor Sizes
 Why pixel pitch and format matter.
 Read → 
 DoF for Landscape
 Hyperfocal, stacking and the f-stop sweet spot.
 Read → 

 Diffraction FAQ

 What is the sharpest aperture? Usually f/4–f/8 on full frame. Past f/8–f/11 diffraction starts softening detail at the pixel level.

 Is f/16 unusable? No. At print sizes the softening is invisible; f/16 is fine when you need maximum depth of field and can't stack.

 Do phone cameras diffract? Yes, and much earlier — a 48 MP phone sensor is diffraction-limited around f/1.8–f/2. That's why phone lenses stay wide open.

SOURCE: https://shuttermath.com/pages/shutter-speed-chart.html
TITLE: Shutter Speed Chart | ShutterMath
SUMMARY: Printable shutter speed chart: freeze birds in flight, pan a race car, smooth a waterfall, or follow the 180-degree video rule. Recommended speeds for every.

Home › Guides › Shutter Speed Chart 
 Shutter Speed Chart

 The shutter speed that freezes your subject depends on how fast it moves across the frame — not just its real speed. These are proven starting points; check sharpness at 100% and adjust.

 Freeze or blur: recommended speeds

 Subject Recommended Notes 

 Birds in flight 1/2000 – 1/4000 s Fast wings need the fastest speeds; use burst + tracking 

 Motorsport / racing 1/1000 – 1/2000 s Or 1/60 – 1/125 s for a panning shot with blurred background 

 Ball sports (tennis, soccer) 1/1000 – 1/2000 s Ball in frame = go faster 

 Kids & pets playing 1/500 – 1/1000 s Unpredictable movement; fast enough to save candid shots 

 Street / documentary 1/250 s Freezes walking subjects; wide enough for available light 

 Portraits 1/125 – 1/250 s People pose; this beats camera shake with stabilization 

 Handheld landscapes 1/focal length (or 2× for APS-C) With stabilization you can go 2–4 stops slower 

 Macro (handheld) 1/200 s or faster Magnification amplifies shake — see the macro guide 

 Waterfall — silky 1/2 – 2 s Tripod + ND filter; use the ND calculator 

 Waterfall — frozen 1/500 – 1/1000 s Bright day, fast shutter 

 City lights / night 2 – 30 s Tripod; bulb mode for longer 

 Star points (astro) see 500/NPF rule Max time before trails — use the star calculator 

 Video: the 180° rule

 For video, shutter is set by the 180° rule: 1/(2 × frame rate) . The full math is in the shutter angle calculator :

 Frame rate 180° shutter 

 24 fps 1/48 s 

 30 fps 1/60 s 

 60 fps 1/120 s 

 120 fps (slow-mo) 1/240 s 

 Handheld rule of thumb

 The classic anti-shake rule: shutter ≥ 1 ÷ focal length (35 mm equivalent). A 200 mm lens needs ≥ 1/200 s; a 24 mm can go as slow as 1/24 s. Modern image stabilization buys you 2–4 extra stops — but only for your shake, not subject movement.

 Related tools & guides

 Exposure Equivalence
 Trade shutter for aperture/ISO without changing brightness.
 Open → 
 ND Filter Calculator
 Get slow shutter speeds in daylight.
 Open → 
 Sports & Action DoF
 Pair the right shutter with the right aperture.
 Read → 

 Shutter speed FAQ

 Why do I need a faster shutter for a flying bird than a running dog? It's about speed across the frame, which depends on distance and lens magnification too. A bird at 10 m with a 400 mm lens crosses the frame much faster than a dog at 5 m with a 35 mm lens — hence 1/2000+.

 Is a slower shutter ever better? Yes — when you want motion blur: panning with a car (1/60–1/125 s), silky water (1/2–2 s), light trails (seconds), or intentional camera movement. Blur tells the story of motion; freezing erases it.

 Does image stabilization let me ignore the rule? For static subjects, yes — you can go 2–4 stops slower handheld. For moving subjects, no: stabilization counters your shake, not the subject's motion. Keep the subject speed, not the rule.
